cards.title: Evolution is a non-directional process of change in heritable characteristics…
cards.subject: Biology
cards.definition: Evolution is a non-directional process of change in heritable characteristics of populations over generations driven by natural selection, genetic drift, and mutation, where adaptations arise for immediate environmental fitness rather than progress toward a predetermined "higher" or "more complex" form. Evolution does not imply improvement, complexity increase, or movement toward a goal; it only produces organisms better suited to their current specific environment.
steps: Observe a bacterium and a human being — both are alive today, both have survived 3.5 billion years of evolutionary history
Ask: "Which one is more evolved?" Most students instinctively say "human" because we have complex brains, language, technology
But the bacterium has also survived every mass extinction, thrives in environments from Antarctic ice to hot springs to human guts, and reproduces in 20 minutes
Connect this to Class 9 learning about adaptations (c9_bio_ch4_6) — adaptations are always relative to current environment, not absolute improvements
The key principle: natural selection has no foresight, no goal, no memory of "progress" — it only filters variations that work right now in this environment.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "evolution means improvement" or "humans are the peak of evolution") reveals the student holds the linear "ladder of progress" misconception instead of understanding branching, non-directional evolution.
remember: State the precise scientific definition of "evolution" as used in modern biology, and explain why the phrase "evolution is progress toward higher forms" is biologically incorrect.
A student argues: "Bacteria are primitive and simple, while humans are advanced and….
The Antarctic icefish (Channichthyidae) lacks hemoglobin and red blood cells — traits considered "simpler" than the complex oxygen-transport system of temperate….

cards.title: A chemical change (chemical reaction) is a process in which one or more…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: A chemical change (chemical reaction) is a process in which one or more substances (reactants) undergo a transformation to form one or more new substances (products) with different chemical compositions and properties, accompanied by observable signs such as evolution of gas, formation of precipitate, change in colour, change in temperature, or change in state.
steps: Begin with a real-world observation: a student notices a white deposit on the bathroom tiles (limescale) that fizzes when vinegar is poured on it — bubbles appear, the solid disappears, and the solution warms slightly

Ask: "What tells you a chemical reaction happened here?" Connect to Class 6/7 knowledge of physical vs chemical changes (c6_chemistry_ch05_001, c6_chemistry_ch05_002) and indicators of chemical change (c7_chem_ch02_012)
Guide the student to list the five observable signs, emphasizing that each sign corresponds to a change at the particle level (new bonds forming, energy changes)
Conclude by showing the reaction of magnesium ribbon burning in air: bright white light (energy), white ash (new solid product), and mass increase — all signs of a chemical change.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer reveals the student confuses dissolution (physical) with chemical reaction, and does not recognize gas evolution as evidence of new substance formation.
remember: A student adds dilute hydrochloric acid to zinc granules in a test….
When barium chloride solution is mixed with sodium sulphate solution, a white precipitate forms….
A few crystals of copper sulphate (blue) are heated in a test….

cards.title: A chemical equation is a symbolic representation of a chemical reaction where…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: A chemical equation is a symbolic representation of a chemical reaction where reactants (starting substances) are written on the left side and products (new substances formed) on the right side, separated by an arrow (→), with physical states indicated in parentheses. Balancing by inspection is the method of adjusting stoichiometric coefficients (numbers placed before formulas) to ensure the number of atoms of each element is identical on both sides, obeying the Law of Conservation of Mass.
steps: Observe a magnesium ribbon burning in air — it produces a blinding white light and leaves a white ash (magnesium oxide)
This is a chemical change you saw in Class 6 (c6_chemistry_ch05_004) and Class 9 (c9_chem_ch3_1)
To represent it chemically, we first write the word equation: Magnesium + Oxygen → Magnesium oxide
Then we convert to formulas using valency rules from Class 9 (c9_chem_ch3_6): Mg + O₂ → MgO
Notice oxygen atoms are unbalanced (2 on left, 1 on right)
We balance by placing coefficient 2 before MgO, then 2 before Mg: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like H₂ + O₂ → H₂O reveals the student recalls the reaction but fails to apply the Law of Conservation of Mass — they have not balanced oxygen atoms (2 on left, 1 on…
remember: Write the balanced chemical equation for the reaction: Hydrogen gas burns in oxygen gas to form liquid water. Include physical states.
A student writes the skeleton equation for heating calcium carbonate as: CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) +….
Balance the following skeleton equation by inspection: Fe(s) + H₂O(g) → Fe₃O₄(s) + H₂(g). Show all steps and verify the final atom count.

cards.title: A combination reaction is a chemical reaction in which two or more reactants…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: A combination reaction is a chemical reaction in which two or more reactants (elements or compounds) combine to form a single product. The general form is A + B → AB, where A and B can be elements or compounds, and AB is always a compound.
steps: Begin with a real-world observation: a student lighting a magnesium ribbon in the school laboratory sees an intense white flame and a white powdery ash (MgO)
Ask: "What happened to the magnesium and the oxygen from the air?" Connect to prior node c10_chem_cbse_01_001 (identifying chemical change) — new substance formed, energy released
Then use c10_chem_cbse_01_002 (balancing equations) to write the skeletal equation Mg + O₂ → MgO and balance it step-by-step
Highlight that two reactants (Mg, O₂) form ONE product (MgO) — this is the defining pattern
Extend to other examples: burning coal (C + O₂ → CO₂), quicklime reacting with water (CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂)
Emphasize that combination reactions are often exothermic (release heat), linking to the flame observed.
remember: Define a combination reaction and give the general symbolic representation. Provide one example with a balanced chemical equation including physical states.
Why is the reaction CaO(s) + H₂O(l) → Ca(OH)₂(aq) classified as a combination reaction, even though one reactant is a compound and the product is a….
Balance the following combination reaction and identify the type of each reactant (element/compound): Fe(s) + S(s) → FeS(s) Then, if 56 g of iron reacts with 32 g of sulphur….

cards.title: A decomposition reaction is a chemical reaction in which a single compound…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: A decomposition reaction is a chemical reaction in which a single compound breaks down into two or more simpler substances (elements or compounds) under the influence of heat, light, or electricity. The general form is AB → A + B.
steps: Start with a real-world observation: When you heat green ferrous sulphate crystals in a test tube, they turn reddish-brown and release a gas with a choking smell (like in the school lab)
This is thermal decomposition
Then connect to prior concept: In combination reactions (c10_chem_cbse_01_003), two substances combine
here, one substance breaks apart
Show how to identify the energy source: heat (Δ), electric current, or light (hν)
End with the key reaction: 2FeSO₄(s) → Fe₂O₃(s) + SO₂(g) + SO₃(g) (thermal decomposition of ferrous sulphate).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., A + B → AB) reveals confusion with combination reactions.
remember: What is the general representation of a decomposition reaction? Write the symbolic equation.
Why does the decomposition of silver chloride require light, while calcium carbonate requires heat? Explain the difference in energy sources.
Balance the following equation for the thermal decomposition of lead nitrate: Pb(NO₃)₂(s) → PbO(s) + NO₂(g) + O₂(g). Identify the type of decomposition.

cards.title: A displacement reaction is a chemical reaction in which a more reactive element…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: A displacement reaction is a chemical reaction in which a more reactive element displaces a less reactive element from its compound, following the general pattern: A + BC → AC + B (where A is more reactive than B). This occurs for both metals (using the metal reactivity series) and non-metals like halogens (using the halogen reactivity series).
steps: Imagine dropping an iron nail into a blue copper sulphate solution — within minutes, the blue colour fades and a reddish-brown coating appears on the nail
This is a classic displacement reaction where iron (more reactive) pushes copper (less reactive) out of its compound
Start by observing such colour changes or gas evolution in simple test-tube experiments
Connect this to the reactivity series learned in Class 9 (c9_chem_ch3_6) and the concept of chemical change from c10_chem_cbse_01_001
The key step is comparing positions in the reactivity series: only an element above the displaced element can displace it
End by writing the general pattern A + BC → AC + B and noting that the reaction is always accompanied by a visible change (colour, precipitate, gas, temperature).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., writing AB + C → AC + B or saying B is more reactive) reveals the student has memorised the pattern without understanding the reactivity requirement — they will incorrectly predict reactions like Cu + FeSO₄ → CuSO₄ + Fe.
remember: What is the general chemical equation pattern for a single displacement reaction, and which element must be more reactive for the reaction to occur.
A student adds zinc granules to iron(II) sulphate….
Write the balanced chemical equation for the reaction when chlorine gas is bubbled through potassium iodide….

cards.title: A double displacement reaction is a chemical reaction in which two ionic…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: A double displacement reaction is a chemical reaction in which two ionic compounds in aqueous solution exchange their positive and negative ions to form two new compounds, typically resulting in the formation of a precipitate, a gas, or water. The general form is AB(aq) + CD(aq) → AD(s/g/aq) + CB(s/g/aq), where A and C are cations and B and D are anions.
steps: Imagine you add a few drops of colourless silver nitrate solution to a colourless sodium chloride solution in a test tube — you instantly see a white curdy precipitate of silver chloride forming
This is a classic double displacement reaction where ions swap partners
Start by observing that both reactants are soluble ionic compounds (recall solubility rules from Class 9 separation techniques)
The driving force is the formation of an insoluble solid (precipitate), a gas that bubbles out, or water in neutralisation
Connect this to the ion exchange concept from Class 9 ionic bonding (c9_chem_ch3_5) and the law of conservation of mass (c9_chem_ch3_1) to balance the equation
The key reaction pattern is: cation₁ + anion₁ + cation₂ + anion₂ → cation₁ + anion₂ + cation₂ + anion₁.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer such as "formation of a soluble product" or "change in colour only" reveals the student does not understand the thermodynamic driving force — they are focusing on superficial changes rather than the removal of ions from solution as a…
remember: What is the general chemical equation for a double displacement reaction, and what are the three common observable outcomes that drive this reaction forward.
When aqueous solutions of barium chloride and sodium sulphate are mixed, a white precipitate….
A student mixes 5.0 g of sodium carbonate (Na₂CO₃) with excess calcium chloride (CaCl₂)….

cards.title: Oxidation is the gain of oxygen or loss of hydrogen by a substance…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Oxidation is the gain of oxygen or loss of hydrogen by a substance, or the loss of electrons by an atom/ion; reduction is the loss of oxygen or gain of hydrogen by a substance, or the gain of electrons by an atom/ion. In every redox reaction, oxidation and reduction occur simultaneously — the substance that loses electrons (oxidised) is the reducing agent, and the substance that gains electrons (reduced) is the oxidising agent.
steps: Begin with a real-world observation: an iron nail left in the rain develops a reddish-brown coating (rust), while a copper vessel turns green over time
Both are chemical changes students saw in Class 6 (c6_chemistry_ch05_003) and Class 7 (c7_chem_ch02_005)
Ask: "What is common in rusting iron, burning magnesium ribbon, and respiration in our cells?" All involve oxygen combining with a substance
Then introduce the classical definition: oxidation = gain of oxygen/loss of hydrogen
reduction = loss of oxygen/gain of hydrogen
Use the reaction CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O to show CuO loses oxygen (reduced) and H₂ gains oxygen (oxidised)
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "oxidation is loss of oxygen") reveals the student has memorised the terms backwards — a very common error that leads to misidentifying oxidised/reduced species in every subsequent question.
remember: State the classical definition of oxidation and reduction in terms of oxygen and hydrogen transfer.
In the reaction Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂, explain why Fe₂O₃ is said to be reduced and CO is oxidised, using the classical definition.
Identify the oxidised and reduced species in the reaction: Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu. Use the electronic definition (electron transfer).

cards.title: A redox reaction is a chemical reaction in which oxidation (loss of electrons…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: A redox reaction is a chemical reaction in which oxidation (loss of electrons or increase in oxidation state) and reduction (gain of electrons or decrease in oxidation state) occur simultaneously; the substance that gets oxidised is the reducing agent and the substance that gets reduced is the oxidising agent.
steps: Observe an iron nail left in the open during monsoon — it develops a reddish-brown coating (rust)

This is the same rusting you studied in Class 6 (c6_chemistry_ch04_003) and Class 7 (c7_chem_ch01_007), but now we see it as a redox process: iron metal loses electrons (oxidation) while oxygen from air gains electrons…
In the previous node (c10_chem_cbse_01_007) you learned the definitions of oxidation and reduction separately
here we connect them — every electron lost by one species must be gained by another, so the two half-processes happen at the same time in the same reaction
We will break down the overall reaction into two half-reactions to see the electron transfer clearly.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., saying CuO is oxidised) shows the student cannot track oxidation state changes or confuses the direction of electron transfer.
remember: Define a redox reaction and state what happens to the oxidising agent and the reducing agent during the reaction.
In the reaction: CuO(s) + H₂(g) → Cu(s) + H₂O(l), identify which substance is oxidised and which is reduced. Explain why this reaction is a redox reaction.
Write the two half-reactions for the reaction: Zn(s) + CuSO₄(aq) → ZnSO₄(aq) + Cu(s). Show the electron transfer explicitly.

cards.title: Corrosion is the gradual deterioration of a metal due to electrochemical…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Corrosion is the gradual deterioration of a metal due to electrochemical reaction with its environment, primarily oxidation by atmospheric oxygen in the presence of moisture, forming metal oxides/hydroxides. For iron, this process is called rusting, producing hydrated iron(III) oxide (Fe₂O₃·xH₂O) through a redox reaction where iron loses electrons (oxidation) and oxygen gains electrons (reduction) in an aqueous electrolyte.
steps: Observe a rusted iron gate or a green-coated copper statue in your neighborhood — both are familiar examples of metals "rotting" due to oxidation
Recall from Class 6 (c6_chemistry_ch04_003) that rusting requires both air and water, and from Class 10 (c10_chem_cbse_01_007) that oxidation is electron loss
Connect these: iron atoms on the surface lose electrons to become Fe²⁺ (oxidation), while dissolved oxygen in water gains those electrons to form OH⁻ (reduction)
The Fe²⁺ and OH⁻ combine and further oxidize to form the flaky, porous rust (Fe₂O₃·xH₂O) that falls off, exposing fresh metal
This electrochemical cycle continues until the metal is consumed

Prevention strategies all aim to break this electron-transfer cycle by blocking contact with electrolyte (paint/oil), providing a sacrificial anode (galvanization), or making the metal the cathode (cathodic protection).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "salt reacts with iron" or "rusting is not redox") shows the student cannot link electrolyte conductivity to redox reaction rate.
remember: Define corrosion and write the chemical formula of rust. State the two essential conditions required for rusting of iron.
Explain why rusting is classified as an oxidation reaction. Why does an iron nail rust faster in salt water than in pure water.
An iron nail is placed in three test tubes: (A) tap water, (B) boiled distilled water with a layer of oil, (C) dry air with anhydrous….

cards.title: Rancidity is the slow oxidation of fats and oils (triglycerides) in food…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Rancidity is the slow oxidation of fats and oils (triglycerides) in food materials by atmospheric oxygen, producing volatile aldehydes, ketones, and carboxylic acids that cause unpleasant smell and taste. It is an undesirable oxidation reaction where the carbon-carbon double bonds in unsaturated fatty acid chains react with oxygen, breaking down into smaller foul-smelling compounds.
steps: Begin with a real-world observation: open a packet of chips or namkeen left exposed to air for two days — the stale, paint-like smell is rancidity
Connect this to the previous node (c10_chem_cbse_01_009) where iron rusts due to oxidation
here, the "rusting" happens in the fatty acids of food
Ask students to recall that fats contain C=C double bonds (from Class 9 covalent bonding) which are vulnerable to attack by oxygen
Guide them to see that rancidity is a slow redox reaction where oxygen is the oxidising agent and the fatty acid is the reducing agent
Conclude by introducing prevention strategies as ways to either remove oxygen, lower temperature, or add substances that sacrifice themselves to oxidation (antioxidants).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like "bacterial decomposition" or "fermentation" reveals the student confuses microbial spoilage (which requires water and microorganisms) with oxidative rancidity (which occurs even in dry, sterile fats due to direct reaction with atmospheric…
remember: What is the chemical process responsible for the development of unpleasant smell and taste in butter left uncovered at room temperature for several days.
Why do polyunsaturated oils (like sunflower oil) become rancid faster than saturated fats (like ghee or coconut oil) under identical storage conditions.
A packet of potato chips is flushed with nitrogen gas before….

cards.title: Acids are substances that release hydrogen ions (H⁺) in aqueous solution…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Acids are substances that release hydrogen ions (H⁺) in aqueous solution, while bases are substances that release hydroxide ions (OH⁻) in aqueous solution. Acids taste sour, turn blue litmus red, and react with metals to produce hydrogen gas; bases taste bitter, feel soapy, turn red litmus blue, and react with acids to form salt and water.
steps: Start with a real-world observation: When you squeeze lemon juice on a cut, it stings
when you use baking soda for heartburn, it gives relief
Both are everyday encounters with acids and bases
Ask students to recall from Class 7 (node c7_chem_ch01_012) that metals react with acids to produce hydrogen gas
Then introduce the Arrhenius definition: acids give H⁺(aq), bases give OH⁻(aq)
Show how to identify acids and bases using indicators (litmus, turmeric) which will be detailed in next nodes
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., defining acid as proton donor without mentioning aqueous solution, or confusing with Lewis definition) reveals the student has not grasped the specific Arrhenius definition required for Class 10 board exams.
remember: Define an acid and a base according to Arrhenius concept. Give one example of each with chemical formula.
Why does dry HCl gas not turn blue litmus red, but aqueous HCl does? Explain using the Arrhenius concept.
A student has three colorless solutions: dilute HCl, dilute NaOH, and….

cards.title: Acid-base indicators are weak organic acids or bases that undergo a reversible…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Acid-base indicators are weak organic acids or bases that undergo a reversible colour change in response to a change in hydrogen ion concentration (pH) of the solution, with the acidic form (HIn) and conjugate base form (In⁻) having distinctly different colours. The colour transition occurs over a specific pH range characteristic of each indicator.
steps: Begin with a kitchen observation: when turmeric (haldi) stains a white kurta and you wash it with soap (basic), the yellow stain turns reddish-brown — this is an acid-base indicator reaction in daily life
Connect this to Class 7 learning (c7_chem_ch02_012) where colour change was taught as a sign of chemical change
Now, introduce the concept that certain natural dyes change colour specifically due to H⁺/OH⁻ concentration, not just any chemical change

Demonstrate with litmus paper (easiest), then move to liquid indicators: phenolphthalein (colourless ↔ pink) for strong base detection, turmeric (yellow ↔ red) for base-specific detection, and china rose (magenta ↔…
End by summarising the colour-change table — this is the core board-exam memory anchor.
cards.misconception: This misconception leads to errors in titration questions where indicator choice depends on pH range, not stoichiometry.
remember: A student dips a strip of blue litmus paper into a colourless solution. The paper turns red. What is the nature of the solution? Name the ion responsible for this colour change.
Phenolphthalein is colourless in acidic solution but turns pink in basic….
You are given three unlabelled test tubes containing dilute HCl, dilute NaOH, and distilled….

cards.title: Olfactory indicators are substances whose characteristic odour changes or…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Olfactory indicators are substances whose characteristic odour changes or disappears in acidic or basic media, allowing detection of acids and bases through smell rather than colour change. Common examples include onion extract (loses smell in base, retains in acid), vanilla essence (loses smell in base, retains in acid), and clove oil (loses smell in base, retains in acid).
steps: Begin with a familiar kitchen observation: when you add baking soda (base) to chopped onions while cooking, the strong onion smell reduces noticeably, but adding lemon juice (acid) does not remove the smell
Connect this to the previous node (c10_chem_cbse_02_002) where colour-changing indicators were introduced — olfactory indicators work on a different sensory modality (smell vs sight)
Demonstrate by preparing onion extract (boil chopped onion in water, filter), then add dilute HCl and NaOH separately to two test tubes containing the extract
Students smell each: the acidic tube retains the onion odour, the basic tube loses it
Repeat with vanilla essence and clove oil
Conclude that all three olfactory indicators lose their characteristic smell in basic medium but retain it in acidic medium, making them useful for visually impaired students.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "it changes colour") reveals the student confuses olfactory indicators with visual indicators and has not grasped the sensory modality difference.
remember: What is the defining characteristic of an olfactory indicator that distinguishes it from litmus or phenolphthalein.
A student adds dilute NaOH to onion extract and observes the smell….
You are given three unlabelled test tubes containing dilute HCl, dilute NaOH, and distilled….

cards.title: When a dilute acid reacts with a reactive metal…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: When a dilute acid reacts with a reactive metal, a displacement reaction occurs where the metal displaces hydrogen from the acid, producing a salt and hydrogen gas. The general reaction is: 2H⁺(aq) + M(s) → Mⁿ⁺(aq) + H₂(g), where M is a metal above hydrogen in the reactivity series.
steps: Imagine dropping a zinc granule into a test tube containing dilute hydrochloric acid — you see bubbles rising rapidly
That effervescence is hydrogen gas, the same gas that makes a 'pop' sound when a burning splint is brought near the tube mouth
This connects to Class 7 where you learned metals react with acids (c7_chem_ch01_012) and Class 9 where you mastered writing chemical formulae (c9_chem_ch3_6)
Start by observing which metals produce bubbles with dilute HCl, then write the word equation, convert to chemical formulae using valency, balance the equation, and finally test the gas
The key insight: only metals above hydrogen in the reactivity series can displace H⁺ from acids.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like Mg + H₂SO₄ → MgSO₄ + H₂ (unbalanced) or Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂ (wrong acid) reveals the student cannot translate the word equation to correct formulae or balance atoms, indicating gaps in valency cross-method (c9_chem_ch3_6) or law of…
remember: Write the balanced chemical equation for the reaction between magnesium metal and dilute sulphuric acid. Name the salt formed.
A student adds dilute HCl to four test tubes containing: (A) zinc granules, (B) copper turnings, (C) iron filings, (D) silver….
Balance the following equation and identify the type of reaction: Al(s) + HCl(aq) → AlCl₃(aq) +….

cards.title: When an acid reacts with a metal carbonate (CO₃²⁻) or metal hydrogencarbonate…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: When an acid reacts with a metal carbonate (CO₃²⁻) or metal hydrogencarbonate (HCO₃⁻), it produces a salt, water, and carbon dioxide gas. The reaction follows the pattern: Acid + Metal Carbonate → Salt + H₂O + CO₂↑ and Acid + Metal Hydrogencarbonate → Salt + H₂O + CO₂↑, with CO₂ evolution confirmed by turning lime water milky.
steps: Observe what happens when you drop a few drops of vinegar (acetic acid) on baking soda (sodium hydrogencarbonate) in your kitchen — vigorous fizzing occurs due to CO₂ gas
This is the same reaction used in soda-acid fire extinguishers and antacid tablets
Recall from node c10_chem_cbse_02_004 that acids with metals produce H₂ gas
here the anion (CO₃²⁻/HCO₃⁻) decomposes to give CO₂ instead
The key is recognising that carbonate ion accepts two H⁺ while hydrogencarbonate accepts one H⁺, leading to different acid mole ratios
Always test the gas by passing it through lime water — a white precipitate (CaCO₃) confirms CO₂.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer where the student writes only NaCl + CO₂ (missing H₂O) reveals they do not understand that the carbonate ion (CO₃²⁻) combines with 2H⁺ to form H₂CO₃ which decomposes to H₂O +…
remember: Write the balanced chemical equation for the reaction between dilute hydrochloric acid and sodium carbonate. Name all three products formed.
Explain why the reaction of sulfuric acid with sodium hydrogencarbonate requires only half the moles of acid compared to sodium carbonate for the same amount of CO₂ production.
A student adds dilute HCl to a white solid….

cards.title: A neutralisation reaction is a chemical reaction in which an acid reacts with a…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: A neutralisation reaction is a chemical reaction in which an acid reacts with a base to form a salt and water, involving the combination of H⁺ ions from the acid and OH⁻ ions from the base to produce H₂O molecules. The general word equation is: Acid + Base → Salt + Water, and the net ionic equation for strong acid-strong base neutralisation is H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l).
steps: Imagine you have severe acidity after eating spicy food — your mother gives you a spoonful of baking soda solution or an antacid tablet
The burning sensation disappears because the base neutralises the excess HCl in your stomach
This is neutralisation in action: H⁺ from acid + OH⁻ from base → H₂O
Start by recalling that acids give H⁺ and bases give OH⁻ in water (c10_chem_cbse_02_001)
Then observe that when you mix HCl and NaOH, the solution becomes warm — this heat comes from H⁺ and OH⁻ combining
Write the molecular equation, then the ionic equation to see the real reaction
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂ (gas) reveals the student confuses neutralisation with acid-metal reaction (c10_chem_cbse_02_004). Writing NaOH + HCl → NaOCl + H₂ shows confusion with redox or…
remember: Write the balanced chemical equation for the reaction between hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide. Name the salt formed.
Why does the temperature of the solution rise when you mix dilute HCl and dilute NaOH, but not when you mix CH₃COOH and NH₄OH.
25 mL of 0.1 M H₂SO₄ is neutralised by 50 mL of NaOH solution. Calculate the molarity of the NaOH solution. Show all steps.

cards.title: Acids react with metal oxides (basic oxides) to form a salt and water…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Acids react with metal oxides (basic oxides) to form a salt and water, while bases react with non-metal oxides (acidic oxides) to form a salt and water; both are neutralisation reactions where the oxide acts as a base or acid respectively, and water is always a product.
steps: Observe a black copper(II) oxide powder placed in a test tube with dilute hydrochloric acid — the black solid disappears and a blue-green solution forms, indicating a reaction has occurred
Recall from c10_chem_cbse_02_006 that neutralisation produces salt and water
here the metal oxide acts as the base

Next, bubble carbon dioxide gas (from a soda bottle or lime kiln observation) through calcium hydroxide solution — the solution turns milky, showing calcium carbonate formation, a reaction of a base with an acidic oxide
Connect both observations: metal oxides are basic, non-metal oxides are acidic, and both undergo neutralisation with their counterparts to give salt + water
Conclude with the general word equations: Acid + Metal Oxide → Salt + Water
cards.misconception: A wrong answer such as writing Cu₂SO₄ or forgetting to balance the equation reveals the student does not apply valency cross-method correctly or treats the oxide as a metal rather than a basic oxide.
remember: Write the balanced chemical equation for the reaction between dilute sulphuric acid and copper(II) oxide. Identify the salt formed.
Explain why carbon dioxide reacts with sodium hydroxide solution but not with hydrochloric acid, even though both are acids/bases.
Balance the following equation and name the salt: Fe₂O₃(s) + HCl(aq) → ______ + ______.

cards.title: pH is the negative logarithm (base 10) of the hydrogen ion concentration in a…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: pH is the negative logarithm (base 10) of the hydrogen ion concentration in a solution, expressed as pH = -log₁₀[H⁺], where [H⁺] is the molar concentration of hydrogen ions (mol L⁻¹). The pH scale ranges from 0 to 14, with pH < 7 indicating acidity, pH = 7 neutrality (at 25°C), and pH > 7 basicity.
steps: Imagine a farmer in Punjab testing his soil with pH paper before sowing wheat — the paper turns yellow, indicating pH around 6, which is slightly acidic and suitable for wheat
In the lab, you have seen universal indicator turn red for hydrochloric acid and blue for sodium hydroxide
This colour change happens because acids release H⁺ ions and bases release OH⁻ ions
The more H⁺ ions, the stronger the acid
But concentrations like 0.0001 M are hard to compare directly, so scientists use a logarithmic scale: each unit change in pH means a tenfold change in [H⁺]
We will learn to convert between [H⁺] and pH using pH = -log[H⁺], and see why a solution of pH 3 has 100 times more H⁺ than pH 5.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "pH 7 is always neutral" or "acidic pH > 7") reveals the student has memorised the scale but not the condition of 25°C or the logarithmic definition, and may confuse the direction of the scale.
remember: Define pH and state the pH range for acidic, neutral, and basic solutions at 25°C.
Why is the pH scale logarithmic? What does a change of one pH unit represent in terms of hydrogen ion concentration.
Calculate the pH of a 0.001 M H₂SO₄ solution, assuming complete dissociation. (Given: log₁₀2 ≈ 0.30).

cards.title: pH is a critical factor in biological and environmental systems: in digestion…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: pH is a critical factor in biological and environmental systems: in digestion, stomach HCl (pH 1.5–3.5) activates pepsin for protein breakdown; in soil, pH 6.5–7.5 optimizes nutrient availability and microbial activity; in oral health, pH below 5.5 causes hydroxyapatite [Ca₅(PO₄)₃OH] demineralization leading to tooth decay.
steps: Observe a farmer testing soil with pH paper before sowing wheat, a student reaching for an antacid after spicy food, and a dentist warning about fizzy drinks
These everyday moments all hinge on pH control
Recall the pH scale (c10_chem_cbse_02_008): acidic solutions have high H⁺ concentration
In the stomach, parietal cells secrete HCl creating pH ~2, activating pepsinogen to pepsin
In soil, H⁺ ions displace nutrient cations (Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺, K⁺) and solubilize toxic Al³⁺
In the mouth, bacteria ferment sugars to lactic acid, dropping plaque pH below 5.5 and dissolving enamel
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., stomach pH 7, critical pH 7) reveals the student has not memorized the specific numerical thresholds that are frequently asked in 1-mark board…
remember: State the typical pH range of the human stomach and the critical pH value below which tooth enamel (hydroxyapatite) begins to demineralize.
Explain why brushing teeth immediately after drinking orange juice (pH ~3.5) can cause more enamel erosion than waiting 30 minutes.
A farmer tests his field and finds soil pH….

cards.title: A family of salts is a group of salts sharing either the same cation (e.g.…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: A family of salts is a group of salts sharing either the same cation (e.g., sodium salts: NaCl, Na₂SO₄, NaNO₃) or the same anion (e.g., chloride salts: NaCl, KCl, NH₄Cl). The pH of a salt solution in water is determined by the hydrolysis of its ions: salts of strong acids and strong bases yield neutral solutions (pH = 7); salts of strong acids and weak bases yield acidic solutions (pH < 7); salts of weak acids and strong bases yield basic solutions (pH > 7).
steps: Observe that table salt (NaCl) solution feels neutral on skin, but washing soda (Na₂CO₃) solution feels soapy and turns red litmus blue, while ammonium chloride (NH₄Cl) solution turns blue litmus red
Start by recalling the neutralisation reaction (c10_chem_cbse_02_006) where acid + base → salt + water
Identify the parent acid and base for each salt: NaCl comes from HCl (strong acid) and NaOH (strong base)
Na₂CO₃ comes from H₂CO₃ (weak acid) and NaOH (strong base)
NH₄Cl comes from HCl (strong acid) and NH₄OH (weak base)
Connect to pH scale (c10_chem_cbse_02_008): the conjugate ions (CO₃²⁻, NH₄⁺) react with water (hydrolysis) to produce OH⁻ or H⁺, shifting pH
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like "chloride family" or "sulphate family" reveals the student is focusing on the anion instead of the cation, or cannot identify the common ion in the chemical formulae.
remember: Name the family of salts to which Na₂SO₄, NaNO₃, and NaCl belong. What is the common ion.
A student tests the pH of three salt solutions: potassium nitrate (KNO₃), ammonium acetate (CH₃COONH₄), and sodium carbonate….
Write the hydrolysis reaction for the acetate ion (CH₃COO⁻) in water and use it to explain why a solution of sodium acetate (CH₃COONa) has pH >….

cards.title: The chlor-alkali process is the industrial electrolysis of concentrated aqueous…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: The chlor-alkali process is the industrial electrolysis of concentrated aqueous sodium chloride (brine) to produce sodium hydroxide (NaOH), chlorine gas (Cl₂) at the anode, and hydrogen gas (H₂) at the cathode. The overall reaction is 2NaCl(aq) + 2H₂O(l) → 2NaOH(aq) + Cl₂(g) + H₂(g), where NaOH remains in solution and the two gases are collected separately.
steps: Start with a real-world observation: when you sprinkle common salt (NaCl) on a cut lemon, nothing dramatic happens, but pass electricity through its concentrated solution and you get a strong base (NaOH) used in soap, a…
Connect this to the previous node on salts (c10_chem_cbse_02_010) where we learned NaCl is a neutral salt from strong acid and strong base
Now, by applying electrical energy, we break that stability
First, identify the ions present in brine (Na⁺, Cl⁻, H⁺, OH⁻)
Then, predict which ions discharge at each electrode using the reactivity series (from Class 9)
Write the half-reactions, combine them for the overall equation, and finally list the commercial uses of each product — this sequence mirrors the CBSE 3-mark question pattern.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., naming "electrolysis of water" or listing oxygen as a product) reveals the student confuses brine electrolysis with water electrolysis, or does not recall that Cl⁻ discharges preferentially over OH⁻ at the anode in concentrated brine.
remember: What is the name of the industrial process used to produce sodium hydroxide from common salt, and what are the three main products formed.
During the electrolysis of concentrated aqueous NaCl, chlorine gas is produced at the anode instead of….
Write the balanced half-reactions at the cathode and anode, and the overall balanced equation for the chlor-alkali….

cards.title: Bleaching powder (CaOCl₂), baking soda (NaHCO₃), washing soda (Na₂CO₃·10H₂O)…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Bleaching powder (CaOCl₂), baking soda (NaHCO₃), washing soda (Na₂CO₃·10H₂O), and plaster of Paris (CaSO₄·½H₂O) are industrially important salts derived from common salt (NaCl) and other raw materials, each with distinct chemical compositions, preparation methods, and specific applications in daily life and industry.
steps: Imagine you are in a kitchen: baking soda makes dhokla fluffy, washing soda removes stubborn stains from clothes, bleaching powder keeps the water tank clean, and plaster of Paris sets a broken arm
Start by observing that all four are white powders but behave differently with water and heat

Connect to the chlor-alkali process (previous node c10_chem_cbse_02_011) where NaCl gives NaOH, Cl₂, and H₂ — chlorine from this process makes bleaching powder, while NaOH reacts with CO₂ to give baking soda
The key is tracking how the same raw materials yield different salts by controlling reaction conditions.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like "CaCl₂" or "Ca(OCl)₂" reveals confusion between bleaching powder and calcium chloride/calcium…
remember: Write the chemical formula of bleaching powder and state the two raw materials used in its industrial preparation.
Why does baking soda (NaHCO₃) release CO₂ when heated, while washing soda (Na₂CO₃·10H₂O) does not? Explain using the concept of thermal decomposition.
A student heats 16.8 g of baking soda (NaHCO₃) strongly until constant….

cards.title: Physical properties of metals such as metallic lustre (shiny appearance due to…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Physical properties of metals such as metallic lustre (shiny appearance due to reflection of light by free electrons), hardness (resistance to deformation, generally high except for alkali metals), malleability (ability to be beaten into thin sheets without breaking due to non-directional metallic bonding allowing layers of atoms to slide), and ductility (ability to be drawn into thin wires due to the same non-directional bonding) are characteristic properties arising from the metallic bond and the sea of delocalized electrons.
steps: Begin with a real-world observation: a student sees a gold ornament shining (lustre), a blacksmith hammering hot iron into a sheet (malleability), an electrician pulling copper wire through a conduit (ductility), and a…

Connect to Class 8 (c8_chem_ch3_8) where elements were introduced as metals/non-metals, and Class 7 (c7_chem_ch01_002, c7_chem_ch01_003) where malleability and ductility were defined but not explained

Then introduce the electron sea model from Class 9 atomic structure (c9_chem_ch2_6) to explain WHY these properties exist: delocalized electrons act as a "glue" allowing positive ions to slide past each other without…
End with a table of exceptions to memorize for board exams.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like "metals are shiny because they are smooth" reveals the student is recalling a superficial observation without connecting to the electron sea model — a common Class 10 error where students describe appearance but not the electronic cause.
remember: Define metallic lustre and state the atomic-level reason for it in one sentence.
Why are metals generally malleable and ductile while ionic compounds like NaCl are brittle? Explain using the nature of bonding.
A student has four metal samples: sodium (Na), magnesium (Mg), tungsten (W), and mercury….

cards.title: Non-metals are elements that generally lack metallic lustre…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Non-metals are elements that generally lack metallic lustre, are brittle in solid state, have low melting and boiling points, and are poor conductors of heat and electricity; key exceptions include graphite (a form of carbon that conducts electricity due to delocalised electrons), iodine (a lustrous non-metal), diamond (an extremely hard allotrope of carbon), and mercury (a metal that is liquid at room temperature, included here as a contrasting exception to typical metallic properties).
steps: Observe a pencil lead (graphite) completing an electrical circuit in a simple LED tester — it glows, yet pencil lead is made of carbon, a non-metal
Contrast this with a sulphur powder sample that does not conduct
Recall from Class 6 (c6_chemistry_ch04_005) that non-metals are generally poor conductors
Now examine a diamond ring and a mercury thermometer: diamond is the hardest natural substance but a non-metal, while mercury flows like water but is a metal
These exceptions arise from differences in atomic bonding and structure (covalent network vs layered vs metallic bonding)
Connect this to the particle arrangement concepts from Class 8 (c8_chem_ch2_6, c8_chem_ch2_7) to understand how structure dictates properties.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., stating non-metals are lustrous or good conductors) reveals confusion with metallic properties, indicating the student has not distinguished the two classes of elements at a fundamental level.
remember: State the general physical properties of non-metals with respect to: (a) lustre, (b) hardness, (c) electrical conductivity, (d) melting and boiling points, and (e) sonority.
Explain why graphite conducts electricity while diamond, also made of carbon, does not. Use the concept of electron delocalisation in your answer.
A student tests four samples: (A) sulphur powder, (B) graphite rod, (C) iodine crystals, (D)….

cards.title: When metals react with oxygen (from air or pure oxygen)…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: When metals react with oxygen (from air or pure oxygen), they form metal oxides through a combination reaction. The reactivity varies: highly reactive metals (K, Na, Ca, Mg) burn vigorously even at room temperature or on mild heating; moderately reactive metals (Zn, Fe, Cu) require strong heating; noble metals (Au, Pt, Ag) do not react. The general reaction is: Metal + Oxygen → Metal Oxide (e.g., 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO; 4Fe + 3O₂ → 2Fe₂O₃).
steps: Start with a real-world observation: when an iron tawa (griddle) is left on a gas stove, it develops a black coating
when a magnesium ribbon is held in a bunsen burner flame, it burns with a dazzling white light
Ask: "What is common in both?" Both involve metal + oxygen from air
Connect to Class 6 (c6_chemistry_ch04_003: rusting of iron) and Class 7 (c7_chem_ch01_012: reactivity of metals with oxygen)
Then introduce the pattern: group 1, 2 metals react vigorously
transition metals need heat
remember: Write the balanced chemical equation for the reaction of magnesium with oxygen. State the physical state of the product formed.
Copper does not burn in air on strong heating, but iron filings burn vigorously when sprinkled in a flame. Explain this difference using the reactivity series.
A student heats 12 g of magnesium ribbon in a….

cards.title: The reaction of metals with water (cold, hot…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: The reaction of metals with water (cold, hot, or steam) is a redox process where the metal displaces hydrogen from water, forming a metal hydroxide (with cold/hot water) or metal oxide (with steam) and liberating hydrogen gas; the vigour and feasibility of the reaction depend on the metal's position in the reactivity series.
steps: Imagine dropping a small piece of sodium into a trough of cold water — it dances vigorously, catches fire, and the solution turns pink with phenolphthalein
Now contrast this with an iron nail placed in cold water: nothing happens for days, but if you pass steam over red-hot iron in a boiling tube, hydrogen gas is evolved and a black magnetic oxide forms
Begin by recalling the reaction of metals with oxygen (node c10_chem_cbse_03_003) where we saw metals form oxides
here water acts as the oxygen source
Observe that only highly reactive metals (Na, K, Ca) react with cold water, moderately reactive ones (Mg) need hot water, and less reactive ones (Al, Zn, Fe) require steam
This pattern directly builds the reactivity series (node c10_chem_cbse_03_007)
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., writing Mg or Fe) reveals the student cannot distinguish the reactivity thresholds for cold water vs. hot water vs. steam; they likely memorise equations without linking them to the reactivity series.
remember: Name the metal that reacts vigorously with cold water to give a soluble hydroxide and hydrogen gas, and write the balanced chemical equation for the reaction.
Magnesium reacts very slowly with cold water but readily with hot….
Write the balanced chemical equation for the reaction of iron with….

cards.title: Aqua regia is a highly corrosive…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Aqua regia is a highly corrosive, fuming yellow-orange liquid mixture of concentrated nitric acid (HNO₃) and concentrated hydrochloric acid (HCl) in a 1:3 volume ratio. It dissolves noble metals like gold (Au) and platinum (Pt) by combining the oxidizing power of nitric acid with the complexing ability of chloride ions to form soluble chloroaurate (HAuCl₄) or chloroplatinate (H₂PtCl₆) complexes.
steps: Imagine a gold ornament that has lost its shine — you cannot clean it with lemon juice (acid) or any single acid in the school lab
But a jeweler uses a "royal water" (aqua regia) to dissolve the surface layer and restore shine
Start by recalling that gold is placed at the bottom of the reactivity series (c10_chem_cbse_03_007) because it does not react with oxygen, water, or single acids
Then observe that aqua regia is a mixture of two concentrated acids

The breakthrough comes from understanding that HNO₃ oxidizes a small amount of HCl to produce nascent chlorine and nitrosyl chloride (NOCl), which are powerful oxidizing and complexing agents that attack the gold lattice
Finally, write the overall balanced equation showing the formation of chloroauric acid (HAuCl₄).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., 3:1 ratio or listing copper/silver) reveals the student has memorised the name but not the precise composition or the specific metals it affects — a common 1-mark error in board exams.
remember: What is the volume ratio of concentrated nitric acid to concentrated hydrochloric acid in aqua regia, and which two noble metals does it dissolve.
Why does gold not dissolve in concentrated nitric acid alone, nor in concentrated hydrochloric acid alone, but dissolves in aqua regia.
Balance the following chemical equation for the reaction of gold with aqua regia: Au + HNO₃ + HCl → HAuCl₄ + NO + H₂O.

cards.title: A displacement reaction occurs when a more reactive metal displaces a less…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: A displacement reaction occurs when a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from its aqueous salt solution, forming a new salt and the displaced metal. The general reaction is: Metal A + Salt of Metal B → Salt of Metal A + Metal B, provided Metal A is higher in the reactivity series than Metal B.
steps: Observe an iron nail dipped in blue copper sulphate solution — the blue colour fades to light green and a reddish-brown coating appears on the nail
This is a classic displacement reaction where iron (more reactive) pushes copper (less reactive) out of its salt

Start by identifying the two metals involved, recall their relative positions in the reactivity series (introduced in the next node), and apply the rule: a metal higher in the series displaces a metal lower in the…
Write the skeletal equation, balance it, add state symbols (aq for aqueous, s for solid), and note the colour change of the solution and the deposition of the displaced metal
Connect this to the earlier learning in Class 9 about writing chemical formulae (c9_chem_ch3_6) and ionic compounds (c9_chem_ch3_5) to correctly represent the salts.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "any metal can displace any other" or "the metal with higher atomic mass displaces") reveals the student has not grasped the fundamental reactivity principle and is likely guessing based on physical properties rather than chemical…
remember: What is the general condition for a metal to displace another metal from its salt solution.
An iron nail is placed in a solution of zinc sulphate. Will a reaction occur? Explain why or why not using the reactivity series.
Write the balanced chemical equation with state symbols for the reaction when a zinc rod is dipped in lead nitrate solution.

cards.title: The reactivity series is a vertical arrangement of metals in decreasing order…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: The reactivity series is a vertical arrangement of metals in decreasing order of their chemical reactivity, determined by their tendency to lose electrons and form positive ions, as observed through displacement reactions with metal salt solutions, reactions with oxygen, water, and dilute acids.
steps: Begin with a real-world observation: when an iron nail is dipped in copper sulphate solution, the blue colour fades and a reddish-brown coating appears on the nail, but the reverse (copper wire in iron sulphate) shows…
Ask students to recall similar observations from c10_chem_cbse_03_006 (reaction with solutions of other metals)
Connect this to Class 7 learning (c7_chem_ch01_012) where metals were tested with oxygen, water, and acids
Explain that scientists compiled thousands of such observations to create a universal ranking — the reactivity series
End by introducing the standard series: K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb > H > Cu > Ag > Au, emphasizing that hydrogen and carbon are included as reference points for extraction metallurgy.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., placing Cu above Fe, or omitting H) reveals the student has memorised an incomplete list or confused the order of transition…
remember: State the reactivity series of metals including hydrogen and carbon, listing at least ten elements in correct decreasing order of reactivity.
Why is hydrogen placed in the reactivity series of metals even though it is a non-metal? Explain using the concept of electron loss.
A student adds zinc granules to four test tubes containing: (i) MgSO₄, (ii) FeSO₄, (iii) CuSO₄, (iv)….

cards.title: When a metal (typically from Groups 1, 2…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: When a metal (typically from Groups 1, 2, or 13) reacts with a non-metal (typically from Groups 15, 16, or 17), the metal atom loses electrons to form a positively charged cation and the non-metal atom gains those electrons to form a negatively charged anion. The electrostatic attraction between these oppositely charged ions constitutes an ionic bond, resulting in a crystalline ionic compound with a giant three-dimensional lattice structure.
steps: Observe a common kitchen scene: sprinkling table salt (NaCl) on food
Salt is a white crystalline solid formed when sodium (a soft, reactive metal stored under kerosene) reacts violently with chlorine (a poisonous greenish-yellow gas)
How do these two dangerous elements become safe edible salt? Recall from Class 9 (c9_chem_ch3_5) that atoms seek stable octet configurations
Sodium (atomic number 11) has one valence electron
chlorine (atomic number 17) has seven
Sodium loses one electron to achieve neon's configuration (2,8), becoming Na⁺
cards.misconception: A wrong answer where the student shows sharing of electrons (covalent) instead of transfer reveals confusion between ionic and covalent…
remember: Write the electron-dot structure (Lewis structure) for the formation of magnesium oxide (MgO) from magnesium and oxygen atoms. Show only valence electrons.
Why does calcium chloride have the formula CaCl₂ and not CaCl or CaCl₃? Explain using the concept of electron transfer and charge neutrality.
Aluminium (atomic number 13) reacts with nitrogen (atomic number 7) to form aluminium….

cards.title: Ionic compounds are crystalline solids composed of positively charged cations…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Ionic compounds are crystalline solids composed of positively charged cations and negatively charged anions held together by strong electrostatic forces in a three-dimensional lattice; they exist as formula units (e.g., NaCl, MgO) not discrete molecules, and their properties arise from this rigid ionic lattice structure.
steps: Observe a student sprinkling table salt (NaCl) on food — it's a white crystalline solid that dissolves instantly in water but not in oil
In the lab, when the teacher melts NaCl in a crucible and passes current, the bulb glows, but solid NaCl does not conduct
Connect this to the previous node (c10_chem_cbse_03_008) where we saw Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions form a rigid lattice: in solid state ions are fixed, so no conduction
in water, hydration shells pull ions apart making them mobile
melting breaks the lattice giving mobile ions
This explains all three properties from one structural model.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "they are gases" or "weak forces") reveals the student hasn't connected lattice strength to melting point.
remember: State the physical state of ionic compounds at room temperature and give one reason based on their structure.
Why does solid NaCl not conduct electricity, but molten NaCl does? Explain in terms of charge carriers.
A student tests solubility of four compounds: NaCl, MgO, CCl₄, and CH₃COONa. Predict which will dissolve in water and which in kerosene. Justify using polarity.

cards.title: Extraction of metals from their ores involves three main sequential steps…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Extraction of metals from their ores involves three main sequential steps: enrichment (concentration) of the ore to remove unwanted gangue, conversion of the concentrated ore into a metal oxide via roasting (for sulfide ores in excess air) or calcination (for carbonate/hydroxide ores in limited air), and finally reduction of the metal oxide to the free metal using a suitable reducing agent (carbon, CO, or a more reactive metal) based on the metal's position in the reactivity series.
steps: Observe a piece of rusted iron gate (common in Indian monsoons) — the reddish-brown flaky rust is Fe₂O₃·nH₂O, essentially an ore of iron

To get pure iron back, we must reverse nature's process: first separate the rust from sand/soil (enrichment), then ensure it is a pure oxide (roasting/calcination), and finally remove oxygen using a reducing agent in a…

Start by recalling the reactivity series (c10_chem_cbse_03_007): metals low in the series (Hg, Cu) need only heating in air, middle ones (Fe, Zn, Pb) need carbon reduction, and high ones (Al, Mg) need electrolysis

Connect this to the chemical properties of metal oxides studied earlier (c10_chem_cbse_03_003) — metal oxides are basic and can be reduced by carbon because carbon has greater affinity for oxygen at high temperatures.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like "roasting" or writing ZnCO₃ + O₂ → ZnO + CO₂ reveals the student confuses calcination (carbonate decomposition without excess oxygen) with roasting (sulfide oxidation with excess oxygen) and does not recognize that carbonate ores release…
remember: Name the process used to convert zinc carbonate (calamine) ore into zinc oxide. Write the balanced chemical equation.
Why is froth flotation used specifically for sulfide ores (like ZnS, Cu₂S) and not for oxide ores (like Fe₂O₃)? Explain the principle.
A student heats a mixture of copper(II) oxide and carbon powder in a test….

cards.title: Electrolytic refining is the process of purifying impure metal by using it as…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Electrolytic refining is the process of purifying impure metal by using it as the anode in an electrolytic cell where the same metal in pure form deposits on the cathode, while more reactive impurities remain in solution and less reactive impurities fall as anode mud.
steps: Observe the electrical wiring in your home — the copper wires are shiny, reddish-brown, and conduct electricity perfectly
But the copper obtained after extraction (from node c10_chem_cbse_03_010) is only 98-99% pure and contains impurities like Fe, Zn, Ag, Au that reduce conductivity
To get 99.99% pure copper for wires, we use electrolysis
Connect this to the reactivity series (c10_chem_cbse_03_007): metals above copper (more reactive) stay in solution as ions, metals below copper (less reactive) do not oxidise and fall as anode mud
The impure copper block becomes the anode, a thin pure copper strip becomes the cathode, and copper sulphate solution is the electrolyte
When current passes, Cu²⁺ from anode goes into solution and deposits on cathode, leaving impurities behind.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "anode is pure copper" or "electrolyte is water") reveals confusion between the roles of electrodes in electroplating vs refining, or forgetting that the electrolyte must contain the metal ion being refined.
remember: Define electrolytic refining and state the materials used as anode, cathode, and electrolyte for the refining of copper.
In the electrolytic refining of copper, impure copper anode contains iron, zinc, silver, and gold as….
During electrolytic refining of copper, a current of 2.0 A is passed for 30 minutes through the….

cards.title: Corrosion is the gradual destruction of metals by chemical or electrochemical…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Corrosion is the gradual destruction of metals by chemical or electrochemical reaction with their environment. Rusting of iron is a specific type of corrosion where iron reacts with oxygen and water to form hydrated iron(III) oxide (Fe₂O₃·xH₂O), a reddish-brown flaky solid.
steps: Start with a real-world observation: a student sees a rusted iron gate or a bicycle left in the rain
Ask: what changed? Connect to Class 6/7 knowledge that rusting requires air and water
Then introduce the electrochemical view: iron acts as anode, oxygen reduction at cathode, forming Fe²⁺ and OH⁻ which combine to form rust
Show the overall reaction
Then discuss prevention by blocking contact (painting, oiling), sacrificial protection (galvanization with zinc), and cathodic protection
End with the key reaction: 4Fe + 3O₂ + 6H₂O → 4Fe(OH)₃ → 2Fe₂O₃·3H₂O.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., saying it's just a chemical reaction without electron transfer) shows the student has not grasped the electrochemical cell concept introduced in Class 10.
remember: What is the chemical formula of rust, and what are the two essential conditions required for rusting of iron.
Explain why rusting is considered an electrochemical process. What happens at the anode and cathode during rusting.
Write the balanced overall chemical equation for the formation of rust from iron, oxygen, and….

cards.title: Covalent bonding in carbon compounds is the chemical bond formed when carbon…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Covalent bonding in carbon compounds is the chemical bond formed when carbon atoms share one or more pairs of valence electrons with other carbon atoms or atoms of other non-metals (like H, O, N, Cl) to achieve a stable noble gas electron configuration (octet or duplet), resulting in the formation of discrete molecules with definite shapes.
steps: Start with a real-world observation: "When you light a gas stove (methane/CH₄) or use vinegar (acetic acid/CH₃COOH) in cooking, you are using carbon compounds held together by covalent bonds." Connect to Class 9…
Now we focus on carbon — which has 4 valence electrons and cannot easily lose or gain 4 electrons
So it shares." Demonstrate step-by-step: write carbon's electronic configuration (2,4), show it needs 4 more electrons for octet, then draw CH₄ by sharing with four H atoms (each needs 1 electron)
Extend to C-C bonds in ethane, then double bond in ethene, triple in ethyne
Emphasize: each shared pair = one covalent bond
carbon always forms 4 bonds total.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer where the student draws 4 dots around carbon without pairing with H dots reveals they think carbon "gives away" electrons (ionic thinking) or they don't understand each bond is a shared…
remember: Write the electron dot structure of methane (CH₄) showing only the valence electrons. How many shared pairs of electrons are present in one molecule of methane.
Carbon has atomic number 6.….
Draw the electron dot structure of ethyne….

cards.title: Carbon's tetravalency is its ability to form four covalent bonds by sharing its…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Carbon's tetravalency is its ability to form four covalent bonds by sharing its four valence electrons with other atoms. Catenation is the unique ability of carbon atoms to bond with other carbon atoms, forming straight chains, branched chains, and rings of varying sizes. Together, these two properties allow carbon to form millions of distinct organic compounds.
steps: Observe the incredible variety of carbon-based materials around you: the petrol in vehicles, the plastic buckets in your home, the cotton clothes you wear, the medicines you take, and the food you eat (carbohydrates…

Why does carbon form so many compounds while other elements do not? Connect this to the covalent bonding you studied in the previous node (c10_chem_cbse_04_001) and the valency concept from Class 9 (c9_chem_ch2_7)
Carbon has atomic number 6, electronic configuration 2,4
It has 4 valence electrons and needs 4 more to complete its octet
It achieves this by sharing electrons — forming four covalent bonds (tetravalency)
Crucially, carbon can share electrons with other carbon atoms just as easily as with hydrogen or oxygen
cards.misconception: A wrong answer often confuses the two: e.g., "tetravalency is the ability to form chains" or "catenation means carbon has valency…
remember: Define catenation and tetravalency of carbon. How are they different from each other.
Silicon (Si) is in the same group as carbon (Group 14) and also has 4 valence….
Draw the structural formulas (showing all bonds) for the two structural isomers of C₄H₁₀. Name each isomer. Verify that each carbon atom satisfies tetravalency in your structures.

cards.title: Allotropes are different structural forms of the same element in the same…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Allotropes are different structural forms of the same element in the same physical state, exhibiting distinct physical properties due to different arrangements of atoms; carbon exists as diamond (tetrahedral 3D network), graphite (layered hexagonal sheets), and fullerene (spherical C₆₀ cages), all composed solely of carbon atoms.
steps: Begin with a real-world observation: a student holds a pencil "lead" (graphite) and a diamond ring — both are pure carbon, yet one writes smoothly and conducts electricity while the other is the hardest natural…
Connect this to Class 9 covalent bonding (c9_chem_ch3_4) and valency (c9_chem_ch2_7): carbon's tetravalency allows it to form four bonds, but the geometry of those bonds changes everything
Guide the student to visualize sp³ hybridization in diamond (tetrahedral, 109.5°) versus sp² in graphite (trigonal planar, 120°) with delocalized π-electrons between layers
End with fullerene as a curved sp² sheet closing into a soccer-ball cage, showing carbon's versatility.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., saying graphite has 4 sigma bonds) reveals the student confuses total valence electrons with sigma bond count and does not understand that one electron in graphite participates in delocalized π-bonding rather than a localized sigma bond.
remember: Name the type of hybridization and the number of sigma bonds formed by each carbon atom in diamond, graphite, and C₆₀ fullerene.
Explain why graphite conducts electricity but diamond does not, using the concept of electron delocalization and band theory at a Class 10 level.
A student claims that because both diamond and graphite are giant covalent structures, both should have very high melting….

cards.title: Hydrocarbons are organic compounds composed exclusively of carbon and hydrogen…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Hydrocarbons are organic compounds composed exclusively of carbon and hydrogen atoms. Saturated hydrocarbons (alkanes) contain only carbon‑carbon single bonds and follow the general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂; unsaturated hydrocarbons contain at least one carbon‑carbon multiple bond — alkenes have at least one double bond (general formula CₙH₂ₙ) and alkynes have at least one triple bond (general formula CₙH₂ₙ₋₂).
steps: Observe a kitchen LPG cylinder (mostly butane, an alkane), a candle flame (paraffin wax = long‑chain alkanes), a fruit‑ripening pouch (releases ethene, an alkene), and a welder’s torch (uses ethyne/acetylene, an alkyne)
All are hydrocarbons — compounds of only carbon and hydrogen
Recall from c10_chem_cbse_04_001 that carbon is tetravalent and forms covalent bonds
from c10_chem_cbse_04_002 that carbon chains can be straight or branched
Now classify these hydrocarbons by the bond between carbon atoms: only single bonds → saturated (alkanes)
at least one double bond → alkenes
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., C₃H₆ for alkane) reveals the student has memorised formulas without understanding how valency determines the hydrogen count.
remember: Write the molecular formula of the alkane, alkene, and alkyne that each contain exactly three carbon atoms.
Explain why ethene (C₂H₄) is unsaturated while ethane (C₂H₆) is saturated, referring to the type of carbon‑carbon bond and the number of hydrogen atoms attached.
A hydrocarbon has the molecular formula C₅H₁₀. Identify its class (alkane/alkene/alkyne) and draw one possible structural formula showing all bonds.

cards.title: Structural isomerism is a phenomenon where two or more carbon compounds have…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Structural isomerism is a phenomenon where two or more carbon compounds have the same molecular formula but differ in the arrangement of carbon atoms (carbon skeleton) or the position of functional groups/unsaturation along the chain, leading to different structural formulas and distinct physical and chemical properties. For example, butane (C₄H₁₀) exists as n-butane (straight chain) and isobutane (branched chain).
steps: Imagine you have a box of identical Lego bricks (carbon atoms) and you build two different shapes — a straight tower and a branched tree
Both use the same number of bricks (same molecular formula) but their structures differ
In chemistry, carbon's tetravalency and catenation (c10_chem_cbse_04_002) allow it to form chains and branches
Start by drawing the straight-chain version of an alkane (e.g., C₄H₁₀), then systematically move one carbon to create a branch
Check valency: each carbon must have four bonds
This systematic approach prevents missing isomers or drawing duplicates
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "same structure but different formula" or giving stereoisomers) reveals confusion between molecular formula and structural formula, or ignorance of carbon's tetravalency and branching rules.
remember: What is the definition of structural isomers? Give an example with molecular formula C₄H₁₀.
Why does n-pentane have a higher boiling point than neopentane (2,2-dimethylpropane) even though both have the formula C₅H₁₂.
Draw all structural isomers of C₅H₁₂ (alkanes) and name them using IUPAC nomenclature.

cards.title: A functional group is a specific atom or group of atoms in a carbon compound…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: A functional group is a specific atom or group of atoms in a carbon compound that determines its characteristic chemical properties and reactivity, replacing one or more hydrogen atoms in the hydrocarbon chain. For example, the hydroxyl group (–OH) in alcohols, the carbonyl group (–CHO) in aldehydes, the carbonyl group (–CO–) in ketones, and the carboxyl group (–COOH) in carboxylic acids.
steps: Start by showing a student a bottle of hand sanitizer (contains ethanol), a bottle of vinegar (contains ethanoic acid), and a nail polish remover (contains propanone/acetone)

Ask: "What makes these liquids behave so differently even though they are all made of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen?" Connect to prior learning: In Class 9 (c9_chem_ch3_4), you learned carbon forms covalent bonds
Now, observe that replacing just one H atom in methane with –OH gives methanol, which has completely different properties
The key is the functional group – the reactive site
Guide the student to draw structures of ethanol (CH₃CH₂OH), ethanal (CH₃CHO), propanone (CH₃COCH₃), and ethanoic acid (CH₃COOH), circling the functional group in each
End by writing the general formulas: Alcohols (CₙH₂ₙ₊₁OH), Aldehydes (CₙH₂ₙO), Ketones (CₙH₂ₙO), Carboxylic acids (CₙH₂ₙ₊₁COOH).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like "ketone" or "alcohol" reveals the student cannot distinguish the –CHO group (terminal carbonyl with H) from –CO– (internal carbonyl) or –OH. They may be memorizing formulas without recognizing structural features.
remember: Name the functional group present in CH₃CH₂CHO and write its IUPAC name.
Why does ethanol (CH₃CH₂OH) react with sodium metal to produce hydrogen gas, but propanone (CH₃COCH₃) does not.
A compound with molecular formula C₃H₆O gives a positive Tollens' test (silver mirror) but does not react with sodium metal. Identify the compound and write its structural formula.

cards.title: A homologous series is a family of organic compounds having the same functional…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: A homologous series is a family of organic compounds having the same functional group, similar chemical properties, and a gradation in physical properties, where each successive member differs from the previous one by a –CH₂– unit (molecular mass difference of 14 g/mol). The general formula for alkanes is CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, for alkenes CₙH₂ₙ, and for alkynes CₙH₂ₙ₋₂.
steps: Observe an LPG cylinder in an Indian kitchen — it contains mostly butane (C₄H₁₀), while the petrol in a scooter contains octane (C₈H₁₈)
Both are alkanes but differ in physical state and boiling point
This node builds on your knowledge of hydrocarbons (c10_chem_cbse_04_004) and functional groups (c10_chem_cbse_04_006)
We will see how adding a –CH₂– group increases molecular mass, strengthens van der Waals forces, and gradually raises boiling points, while the functional group keeps chemical behaviour similar
By the end, you will predict properties of higher homologues like decane or dodecanoic acid.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ (alkane formula) or C₃H₈ reveals confusion between alkane and alkene general formulas. Writing C₃H₄ (alkyne) shows inability to substitute n=3 correctly.
remember: State the general formula for the homologous series of alkenes and write the molecular formula of the third member of this series.
Explain why the boiling points of alkanes increase steadily as we go down the homologous series from methane to decane, even though their chemical properties remain similar.
The first member of the alcohol homologous series is methanol….

cards.title: IUPAC nomenclature is a systematic method for naming organic compounds by…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: IUPAC nomenclature is a systematic method for naming organic compounds by identifying the longest continuous carbon chain (parent chain), the functional group (which determines the suffix), and the positions of substituents (prefixes) using the lowest set of locants, ensuring each compound has a unique, unambiguous name accepted internationally.
steps: Imagine you are reading the label of a medicine bottle — "Paracetamol" is its common name, but its systematic name is N-(4-hydroxyphenyl)acetamide
Without a universal naming system, chemists worldwide would confuse structures
Start by recalling from node c10_chem_cbse_04_004 that carbon forms chains
The first step is always to count the maximum number of carbon atoms in a continuous chain — that gives the root word (meth, eth, prop...)
Next, check for double/triple bonds or functional groups from node c10_chem_cbse_04_006 to decide the suffix (-ane, -ene, -yne, -ol, -al, -one, -oic acid)
Then number the chain from the end nearest to the functional group or multiple bond
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like "Butylene" or "C4H10" reveals the student confuses the suffix for saturated alkanes (-ane) with unsaturated ones (-ene) or thinks the molecular formula is the…
remember: What is the correct IUPAC name for the compound with the structural formula CH₃-CH₂-CH₂-CH₃.
A student writes the name of CH₃-CH(OH)-CH₃ as….
Write the IUPAC name for the following structure: CH₃-CH(CH₃)-CH₂-CH₂-OH. Show your numbering and identify the root word, suffix, and prefix.

cards.title: Combustion of carbon compounds is an exothermic oxidation reaction where a…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Combustion of carbon compounds is an exothermic oxidation reaction where a carbon-containing compound (hydrocarbon or its derivative) reacts with oxygen to produce carbon dioxide, water vapour, heat, and light. For complete combustion of a hydrocarbon CₓHᵧ: CₓHᵧ + (x + y/4)O₂ → xCO₂ + (y/2)H₂O + heat/light.
steps: Observe a kitchen LPG stove: the blue flame indicates complete combustion of butane (C₄H₁₀) with sufficient air, while a yellow sooty flame on a kerosene stove shows incomplete combustion
Connect this to Class 6 learning that combustion is a chemical change producing heat/light (c6_chemistry_ch05_004)
Now, using your knowledge of hydrocarbon formulas from c10_chem_cbse_04_004 and balancing from c9_chem_ch3_6, write the balanced equation for methane combustion
Notice the pattern: every C becomes CO₂, every H becomes H₂O, and O₂ balances the oxygen atoms
This pattern lets you predict combustion products for any carbon compound.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., C₃H₈ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O unbalanced, or missing states) reveals the student cannot apply the stoichiometric pattern (x CO₂, y/2 H₂O) or recall that water is liquid at room temperature.
remember: Write the balanced chemical equation for the complete combustion of propane (C₃H₈). State the physical states of reactants and products at room temperature.
Explain why ethylene (C₂H₄) burns with a yellow sooty flame while methane (CH₄) burns with a clean blue flame under the same air supply.
2.2 g of propane (C₃H₈) is burnt completely in excess oxygen. Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide produced. (Molar masses: C=12, H=1, O=16 g/mol).

cards.title: Oxidation in carbon compounds is a reaction where a carbon atom gains oxygen or…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Oxidation in carbon compounds is a reaction where a carbon atom gains oxygen or loses hydrogen, typically using an oxidizing agent like alkaline KMnO₄ or acidified K₂Cr₂O₇. Addition reaction occurs in unsaturated hydrocarbons (alkenes/alkynes) where atoms add across the double/triple bond to form a saturated product. Substitution reaction occurs in saturated hydrocarbons (alkanes) where one hydrogen atom is replaced by another atom/group (e.g., halogen) in presence of sunlight.
steps: Observe how cooking oil (unsaturated fat) is converted to solid vanaspati ghee (saturated fat) in Indian kitchens — this is industrial hydrogenation, an addition reaction
Next, recall that ethanol in alcoholic drinks turns sour when left open due to oxidation by air to ethanoic acid (vinegar)
Then, think of chlorine gas reacting with methane in sunlight to give chloromethane — a substitution reaction
Connect these to prior knowledge: unsaturated hydrocarbons have double/triple bonds (node c10_chem_cbse_04_004) and alcohols have -OH functional group (node c10_chem_cbse_04_006)
The key is to recognize the reactant type (saturated vs unsaturated, functional group) and the reagent/condition to classify the reaction.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "concentrated H₂SO₄" or "no color change") reveals confusion between dehydrating agents and oxidizing agents, or ignorance of the visual indicator of oxidation.
remember: Name the oxidizing agent commonly used in the laboratory to oxidize ethanol to ethanoic acid. Write the color change observed during this reaction.
Ethene (C₂H₄) reacts with bromine water (Br₂ in H₂O). What type of reaction is this? Why does the reddish-brown color of bromine water disappear.
Write the balanced chemical equation for the reaction of methane with chlorine in presence of sunlight. Identify the type of reaction and the condition required.

cards.title: Ethanol (C₂H₅OH) is a two-carbon alcohol with a hydroxyl (–OH) functional…
cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.definition: Ethanol (C₂H₅OH) is a two-carbon alcohol with a hydroxyl (–OH) functional group, and ethanoic acid (CH₃COOH) is a two-carbon carboxylic acid with a carboxyl (–COOH) functional group; both are important industrial and laboratory carbon compounds exhibiting characteristic reactions due to their functional groups.
