cards.definition: Word problems on interpreting frequency distribution tables require extracting statistical information (class intervals, frequencies, cumulative frequencies, class marks) from a given table and applying appropriate formulas for mean, median, mode, or graphical methods to answer real-world questions. The process involves identifying the type of distribution (discrete or continuous), determining which measure of central tendency is required, and executing the correct computational method with proper interpretation of results in context.
steps: Imagine your school conducts a health check-up and records the heights of 100 Class 10 students in a frequency table

The principal asks: "What is the average height? What height do most students have? What is the middle height?" You are handed a table with class intervals like 140-145, 145-150, etc., and frequencies
First, write down what is given: the class intervals, frequencies, and total number of students
Next, identify what is asked — mean, median, or mode? If mean, check if class marks are large — if yes, use assumed mean or step-deviation method
If median, find cumulative frequencies and locate the median class
If mode, identify the modal class
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., 140 or 100) reveals the student confuses upper/lower limits or incorrectly identifies the modal class by looking at class marks instead of frequencies.
remember: A frequency distribution table shows the daily wages (in ₹) of 50 workers in a….
In a grouped frequency distribution, the class marks are 15, 25, 35, 45, 55 and the corresponding frequencies are 4, 6, 10, 8….
The following table shows the literacy rate (in %) of 35 cities: | Literacy Rate | 45-55 | 55-65 | 65-75 | 75-85 | 85-95 |….

cards.title: The classical definition of probability states that if an experiment has n…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The classical definition of probability states that if an experiment has n equally likely outcomes and m of them are favourable to an event E, then the probability of event E is P(E) = m/n, where 0 ≤ P(E) ≤ 1. Equally likely outcomes are those that have the same chance of occurring. This definition applies only when all outcomes are equally likely (symmetric, fair conditions) and the sample space is finite.
steps: Imagine tossing a fair coin
There are two possible outcomes: Heads (H) and Tails (T)
Both are equally likely — neither is favoured
The total number of outcomes n = 2
If event E is "getting Heads", the favourable outcomes m = 1
So P(Heads) = 1/2
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., omitting "equally likely") shows the student does not understand the critical condition for the classical definition.
remember: State the classical definition of probability.
What is the probability of drawing a king from a well-shuffled deck of 52 cards.
A bag contains 5 red and 3 blue balls. What is the probability of drawing a red ball.

cards.title: The sample space of a random experiment is the set of all possible outcomes of…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The sample space of a random experiment is the set of all possible outcomes of that experiment, denoted by S or Ω. An event is any subset of the sample space, representing a collection of outcomes to which we assign a probability; an elementary event contains exactly one outcome, while a compound event contains two or more outcomes.
steps: Imagine you are playing a board game with your friends during Diwali holidays: you roll two dice simultaneously to move your token
Before calculating your chances of getting a sum of 7, you must first list every possible outcome when two dice are rolled
Start by asking: "What are all the distinct results that can appear?" Write down the outcomes for one die (1 to 6), then pair each with the outcomes of the second die
This systematic pairing builds the sample space
Connect this to Class 9 where you listed outcomes for a single die or coin
now extend to multiple trials
cards.misconception: A wrong answer would indicate the student confuses "complementary" with "equally likely" or thinks complementary events must have the same number of outcomes (which they do here, but that's not the defining property).
remember: A student writes the sample space for tossing two coins simultaneously as S = {HH, HT….
When rolling a single die, a student defines event E = {2, 4, 6} and event F = {1, 3….
A bag contains 5 red balls numbered 1 to 5 and 3 blue balls numbered 1 to….

cards.title: The probability of an event E, denoted P(E)…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The probability of an event E, denoted P(E), is defined as the ratio of the number of favourable outcomes to the total number of equally likely possible outcomes in the sample space S. Mathematically, P(E) = n(E) / n(S), where n(E) is the number of outcomes favourable to event E and n(S) is the total number of outcomes in the sample space, provided all outcomes are equally likely.
steps: Imagine you are playing a board game with your friends and you need to roll a die to get a 6 to win
You wonder: "What are my chances?" To begin, write down all possible outcomes when a fair die is rolled: {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}
This is your sample space S, so n(S) = 6
The event E is "getting a 6", so favourable outcomes = {6}, giving n(E) = 1
Now apply the formula P(E) = n(E)/n(S) = 1/6

The key insight is that probability is a fraction between 0 and 1, where the denominator is the total number of equally likely outcomes and the numerator counts only those outcomes that satisfy the event.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., writing P(E) = n(S)/n(E) or using "total trials" instead of "total outcomes") reveals confusion between favourable and total outcomes or misunderstanding that the formula applies only to equally likely outcomes.
remember: State the formula for the probability of an event E using the classical definition. Define each symbol used.
A bag contains 5 red balls and 3 blue balls. A student writes P(red) = 5/3. Explain why this is incorrect and state the correct probability.
A die is rolled once. Find the probability of getting a prime number. Show all steps.

cards.title: An elementary event is an event that consists of exactly one outcome of a…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: An elementary event is an event that consists of exactly one outcome of a random experiment. When all outcomes of an experiment are equally likely, the probability of each elementary event is 1/n, where n is the total number of elementary events in the sample space. The sum of the probabilities of all elementary events in a sample space is always 1.
steps: Imagine you are playing a board game with a fair spinner divided into 8 equal sectors numbered 1 to 8
You spin it once — what is the chance it lands on 5? This is an elementary event because "landing on 5" is a single outcome
Since the spinner is fair, all 8 outcomes are equally likely
We first write the sample space S = {1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8} with n(S)=8
The elementary event E = {5} has 1 favourable outcome
Using the classical definition P(E)=1/8
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., listing only 3 outcomes like {HH, HT, TT} or giving probability 1/3) reveals the student does not understand that HT and TH are distinct elementary events when tossing two coins, a classic error from not writing the full sample space.
remember: In a random experiment of tossing two coins simultaneously, list all elementary events and state the probability of each elementary event.
A bag contains 3 red balls, 4 blue balls, and 5 green….
A fair die is rolled once.….

cards.title: For any event E in a random experiment with equally likely outcomes…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: For any event E in a random experiment with equally likely outcomes, the complementary event 'not E' (denoted as E' or Ē) consists of all outcomes in the sample space that are not in E. The sum of the probabilities of an event and its complement is always 1: P(E) + P(not E) = 1, provided the sample space is finite and all outcomes are equally likely.
steps: Imagine you are playing a game of Ludo with your cousins
You need a 6 to start your token
Instead of calculating the probability of getting a 6 directly, think: what is the probability of NOT getting a 6? There are 5 outcomes that are not 6 out of 6 total outcomes
So P(not 6) = 5/6
This is often easier when the complement has fewer outcomes
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like P(E) - P(not E) = 1 or P(E) × P(not E) = 1 reveals the student has memorised an incorrect relationship and does not understand that the event and its complement partition the sample space.
remember: State the formula that relates the probability of an event E and the probability of its complementary event 'not E'.
A student says: "If the probability of rain tomorrow is 0.3, then the probability of no rain is….
A box contains 5 red, 8 blue, and 7 green marbles. One marble is drawn at random. Find the probability that the marble drawn is NOT blue.

cards.title: An impossible event has probability 0…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: An impossible event has probability 0 — it can never occur under any circumstances. A certain event has probability 1 — it must always occur. For any event E, 0 ≤ P(E) ≤ 1, where P(E) = 0 defines an impossible event and P(E) = 1 defines a certain event. These are the two extreme cases of the classical probability definition P(E) = m/n: when m = 0 (no favourable outcomes), P = 0; when m = n (all outcomes are favourable), P = 1.
steps: Roll a standard die numbered 1 to 6
The event "rolling a 7" is impossible — there is no 7 on the die, so m = 0 and P(7) = 0/6 = 0
The event "rolling a number from 1 to 6" is certain — every outcome is favourable, so m = 6 and P(1 to 6) = 6/6 = 1
These are the two extremes
Any event with 0 < P(E) < 1 is a "probable" event — it may or may not occur
For example, P(rolling an even number) = 3/6 = 1/2, which is probable
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "impossible means P < 0") shows the student does not know the bounds of probability.
remember: Define an impossible event and a certain event in terms of probability.
When rolling a die, what is the probability of rolling a number greater than 6.
When drawing a card from a standard 52-card deck, what is the probability of drawing a card that is either red or black.

cards.title: The complement of an event E, denoted E' or "not E"…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The complement of an event E, denoted E' or "not E", is the event that E does NOT occur. The probability of the complement is P(not E) = 1 − P(E). This follows from the fact that the sample space S is partitioned into E and E' (E and not E), so P(E) + P(not E) = P(S) = 1. The complement rule is one of the most useful tools in probability: if computing P(E) directly is difficult, compute P(not E) and subtract from 1.
steps: When you roll a die, the event E = "rolling a 6" has P(E) = 1/6
The complement "not E" = "not rolling a 6" includes {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}, so P(not E) = 5/6
This is the complement rule: P(not E) = 1 − P(E)
The rule is powerful when direct counting is hard
For example, "at least one head in 3 coin tosses" — counting directly (HHH, HHT, HTH, HTT, THH, THT, TTH = 7) is tedious
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "P(not E) = P(E)") shows the student does not understand the relationship between an event and its complement.
remember: State the complement rule for probability.
If P(E) = 0.3, find P(not E).
A die is rolled. What is the probability of NOT getting a prime number.

cards.title: In dice probability word problems…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: In dice probability word problems, the sample space consists of all possible ordered outcomes when one or more fair six-faced dice are rolled. For a single die, the sample space S = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6} with n(S) = 6 equally likely outcomes. For two dice rolled simultaneously (or one die rolled twice), the sample space contains 36 ordered pairs (i, j) where i, j ∈ {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}, giving n(S) = 36. The probability of an event E is calculated as P(E) = n(E)/n(S), where n(E) is the number of favourable ordered outcomes satisfying the given condition.
steps: Imagine you're playing Ludo with your cousins during Diwali vacation
You need a sum of 7 on two dice to move your token home and win the game
Your younger cousin asks: "Didi, what are my actual chances of getting 7?" This is exactly where dice probability word problems begin — with a real situation needing a numerical answer
First, we identify the experiment: rolling two dice simultaneously
The sample space isn't just sums from 2 to 12
it's 36 ordered pairs because (3,4) and (4,3) are different outcomes
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like 1/2 (thinking only 5 and 6 are >4 but forgetting to divide by 6) or 2/36 (using two-dice sample space for a one-die problem) reveals the student cannot distinguish between one-die and two-dice sample spaces or miscounts total outcomes.
remember: A die is rolled once. What is the probability of getting a number greater than 4? Write the sample space and the favourable outcomes explicitly.
Two dice are rolled together.….
Two dice are rolled simultaneously. Find the probability that the product of the numbers appearing on the top faces is a perfect square.

cards.title: Word problems on probability with playing cards involve calculating the…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Word problems on probability with playing cards involve calculating the likelihood of drawing specific cards or types of cards from a well-shuffled standard deck of 52 cards, using the classical probability formula P(E) = n(E)/n(S) where n(S) = 52 and n(E) is the count of favourable cards satisfying the given condition.
steps: Imagine you're playing a card game with friends during Diwali and someone asks: "What are the chances I draw a red king from this shuffled deck?" To begin, write down the total cards = 52
Next, list the card categories: 4 suits × 13 ranks
Identify the favourable cards — red kings are King of Hearts and King of Diamonds = 2 cards

The key insight is systematically breaking down the deck: 26 red, 26 black, 4 of each rank, 12 face cards, 4 aces, 36 number cards — then using set logic (union/intersection) for compound events like "face card or ace".
cards.misconception: A wrong answer of 16/52 or 4/13 reveals the student incorrectly includes Aces as face cards or miscounts suits. An answer of 12/52 without simplification shows incomplete simplification skill.
remember: How many cards are there in a standard deck, and how many of them are face cards? Write the probability of drawing a face card in simplest form.
A student calculates the probability of drawing a "red face card" as 6/52 =….
A card is drawn at random from a well-shuffled deck of 52….

cards.title: Coin tossing probability problems involve calculating the likelihood of…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Coin tossing probability problems involve calculating the likelihood of specific outcomes when one or more fair coins are tossed, where the sample space consists of all equally likely ordered outcomes (Heads or Tails for each coin). For one coin, the sample space is {H, T} with 2 outcomes; for two coins, the sample space is {HH, HT, TH, TT} with 4 outcomes where HT and TH are distinct events.
steps: Imagine you're at a school fair in Delhi where a game stall offers a prize if you toss two coins and get "at least one head"
You wonder: what are your actual chances of winning? To begin, always write down the sample space first — for two coins, list all four ordered pairs: HH, HT, TH, TT
Many students mistakenly write only three outcomes (HH, HT, TT) forgetting that HT and TH are different
Once the sample space is correct, count the favourable outcomes for "at least one head" — that's HH, HT, TH (3 outcomes)
Apply the formula P(E) = 3/4
The key insight: order matters in coin tosses because each coin is distinct, even if they look identical.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like {HH, HT, TT} (only 3 outcomes) reveals the student treats HT and TH as the same outcome, not understanding that the two coins are distinct — even if identical in appearance, the first coin showing H and second T is different from first T…
remember: What is the sample space when two fair coins are tossed simultaneously? List all outcomes.
Explain why the probability of getting "at least one head" when two coins are tossed is 3/4, not 2/3.
Two fair coins are tossed. Find the probability of getting: (i) exactly one head, (ii) at most one tail, (iii) no head.

cards.title: Probability in real-life situations applies the classical definition P(E) = m/n…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Probability in real-life situations applies the classical definition P(E) = m/n to practical scenarios: weather prediction, quality control, games of chance, medical testing, survey analysis, and decision-making. The process involves: (1) identifying the random experiment, (2) listing the sample space, (3) counting favourable and total outcomes, (4) computing P(E) = m/n, and (5) interpreting the result in context. When direct counting is difficult, the complement rule P(not E) = 1 − P(E) is used.
steps: Real-life probability problems follow a standard template
Example: "A factory produces 1000 bulbs, 50 are defective
If one is selected at random, what is the probability it is good?" Step 1: Experiment = selecting one bulb
Step 2: n = 1000
Step 3: Favourable (good) = 1000 − 50 = 950
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., 20/500 = 1/25) shows the student computed P(defective) instead of P(non-defective).
remember: A factory produces 500 items, 20 of which are defective. What is the probability that a randomly selected item is non-defective.
In a class of 40 students, 25 play cricket and 15 play football. If one student is selected at random, what is the probability that the student plays cricket.
A weather forecast says there is a 60% chance of rain tomorrow. Interpret this in terms of probability.

cards.title: Electric current is the rate of flow of electric charge through a conductor.
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Electric current is the rate of flow of electric charge through a conductor. It is defined as the amount of charge (Q) passing through a cross-section of a conductor per unit time (t). The SI unit of electric current is the ampere (A), where 1 ampere = 1 coulomb per second (1 A = 1 C/s). Conventional current direction is taken as the direction of flow of positive charge, which is opposite to the actual flow of electrons in a metallic conductor.
steps: Observe a ceiling fan in your classroom: when you flip the switch, the fan starts rotating almost instantly
This happens because electric charge begins to flow through the wires the moment the circuit is closed
You already know from Class 6 (c6_physics_ch03_012) and Class 7 (c7_physics_ch02_006) that a closed circuit with a cell allows current to flow
Now we quantify that flow: how much charge passes a point per second
We start by measuring charge in coulombs (learned in Class 8, c8_physics_ch2_6) and time in seconds
The key principle is that current is a rate — just like speed is distance per time, current is charge per time
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "current is the flow of electrons" without mentioning rate, or "unit is coulomb") reveals the student confuses current with charge or does not grasp the "rate" concept. They may also forget the conventional current direction.
remember: Define electric current and state its SI unit. What does 1 ampere represent in terms of charge and time.
In a metallic wire, electrons flow from the negative terminal to the positive terminal of a….
A charge of 300 coulombs passes through a cross-section of a wire in 5 minutes. Calculate the electric current in amperes. Show all steps with units.

cards.title: Electric potential at a point in an electric field is the work done per unit…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Electric potential at a point in an electric field is the work done per unit positive charge in bringing that charge from infinity to that point without acceleration. Electric potential difference (voltage) between two points is the work done per unit charge in moving a positive charge from one point to the other. The SI unit is volt (V), where 1 V = 1 J/C. This is a scalar quantity, and potential difference is measured by a voltmeter connected in parallel across the component.
steps: Observe a battery-powered LED torch: when you press the switch, the LED glows because charges move through it
What makes charges move? In Class 6 (c6_physics_ch03_016), you learned a cell provides "push" — now we name that push: potential difference
Begin by recalling from Class 9 (c9_physics_ch4_1) that work is done when a force moves an object
Here, the electric force does work on charges
Measure the work done (in joules) to move a known charge (in coulombs) between two points in a circuit using a laboratory power supply and a coulomb meter
The ratio W/Q gives the potential difference in volts
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "V = Q/W" or unit as "ampere") reveals the student has memorised the formula incorrectly or confuses potential difference with current — a common board exam error where students swap numerator and denominator.
remember: Define electric potential difference and state its SI unit. Write the formula relating potential difference, work done, and charge.
A student says: "Potential difference is the same as electric potential." Is this correct? Explain why or why not using the concept of reference point.
A charge of 50 C is moved between two points in a circuit. If the work done is 600 J, calculate the potential difference between the points. Show all steps with units.

cards.title: Ohm's Law states that the electric current flowing through a conductor is…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Ohm's Law states that the electric current flowing through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference applied across its ends, provided the temperature and other physical conditions of the conductor remain constant. Mathematically, \( V = IR \), where \( V \) is the potential difference in volts (V), \( I \) is the current in amperes (A), and \( R \) is the resistance in ohms (Ω). The V-I graph for an ohmic conductor is a straight line passing through the origin, with slope equal to resistance.
steps: Begin with a real-world observation: a student switches on a desk fan and notices the speed changes when the regulator is turned
The regulator changes the potential difference across the fan's motor, which changes the current
Connect to prior concepts: from c10_phy_cbse_01_001, current is the flow of charge
from c10_phy_cbse_01_002, potential difference is the "push" that drives the current

Now, ask: "If we increase the push (V), what happens to the flow (I)?" Guide students to set up a simple circuit with a nichrome wire, ammeter, voltmeter, and a variable power supply (or cells in series)
Measure V and I for at least 5 settings, record in a table, and plot V (y-axis) vs I (x-axis)
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "V = I/R" or missing the constant temperature condition) reveals the student has memorised the formula without understanding the physical condition or the direct proportionality relationship.
remember: State Ohm's Law in words and write its mathematical formula. What is the SI unit of each quantity in the formula.
A student plots a V-I graph for a nichrome wire and gets a straight line passing through the origin with a slope of 5….
An electric iron draws a current of 4.5 A when connected to a 220 V mains supply. Calculate the resistance of the iron's heating element. Show all steps with units.

cards.title: Resistance is the property of a conductor that opposes the flow of electric…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Resistance is the property of a conductor that opposes the flow of electric current through it. It is defined as the ratio of the potential difference (V) across the conductor to the current (I) flowing through it, provided the physical conditions (temperature, dimensions) remain constant. The SI unit of resistance is the ohm (Ω), where 1 Ω = 1 V/A.
steps: Observe a household electric iron: when you switch it on, the heating element becomes hot because it resists the current
Start by recalling from Class 8 (c8_physics_ch2_7) that heat produced depends on current, resistance, and time
Now, connect to Ohm's law (c10_phy_cbse_01_003): V = IR, so resistance R = V/I
Measure voltage across a wire and current through it using a voltmeter and ammeter in a school lab circuit
Notice that thicker wires (larger cross-section) allow more current for the same voltage, meaning lower resistance
Longer wires of the same material show higher resistance
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "watt" or "ampere") reveals the student confuses resistance with power or current. If the student writes R = I/V, they have inverted the Ohm's law relationship.
remember: What is the SI unit of resistance? Define resistance in terms of potential difference and current.
A student says: "If I increase the length of a wire, its resistance decreases because the current has more space to flow." Explain why this statement is incorrect using the….
A nichrome wire of length 2 m and cross-sectional area 0.5 mm² has a resistance of 10 Ω when a potential difference of 5 V is applied across….

cards.title: Resistivity (ρ) is an intrinsic property of a material that measures how…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Resistivity (ρ) is an intrinsic property of a material that measures how strongly it opposes the flow of electric current. It is defined by the formula ρ = R × A / L, where R is resistance, A is the cross-sectional area, and L is the length of the conductor. The SI unit of resistivity is the ohm-metre (Ω·m). Resistivity is independent of the dimensions of the conductor — it depends only on the material and temperature. Conductors (like copper, ρ ≈ 1.68 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m) have low resistivity, insulators (like rubber, ρ ≈ 10¹³ Ω·m) have high resistivity, and alloys (like nichrome, ρ ≈ 1.10 × 10⁻⁶ Ω·m) have intermediate resistivity.
steps: Imagine two copper wires: one thick and short, one thin and long
Both are copper, so they have the SAME resistivity
But the thin, long wire has MORE resistance because resistance depends on dimensions (R = ρL/A)
Resistivity is like "density" — it is a property of the material itself, not the object
Copper always has resistivity 1.68 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m whether the wire is 1 cm or 1 km long
To find resistivity experimentally: measure R (with a multimeter), measure L (with a ruler) and A (from the wire's diameter), then compute ρ = RA/L
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "resistivity is the same as resistance") shows the student does not distinguish between the two concepts.
remember: Define resistivity and state its SI unit.
Two wires of the same material have the same length but different cross-sectional areas A₁ = 2A₂. How do their resistivities compare.
A wire of length 2 m and cross-sectional area 1 × 10⁻⁶ m² has resistance 3.4 Ω. Find the resistivity of the material.

cards.title: In a series combination of resistors…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: In a series combination of resistors, the same current flows through each resistor connected end-to-end in a single path, and the equivalent resistance (R_s) is the arithmetic sum of individual resistances: R_s = R_1 + R_2 + R_3 + ... . The total potential difference across the combination equals the sum of potential differences across each resistor (V = V_1 + V_2 + V_3 + ...). SI unit of equivalent resistance is ohm (Ω).
steps: Observe a string of decorative LED lights used during Diwali — if one bulb fuses, the entire string goes dark because they are connected in series
Start by recalling Class 6 knowledge that series circuits have only one path for current (c6_physics_ch03_017)
Connect to Ohm's law (c10_phy_cbse_01_003): since current I is same everywhere, the total voltage V = IR_1 + IR_2 + IR_3 = I(R_1+R_2+R_3)
Thus the equivalent resistance R_s = V/I = R_1+R_2+R_3
Emphasize that adding resistors in series increases total resistance, reducing current for a given voltage
End with the key formula: R_s = R_1 + R_2 + R_3 + ...
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like 1/10 Ω or 30 Ω reveals the student is confusing series formula with parallel formula or multiplying resistances instead of adding.
remember: Three resistors of 2 Ω, 3 Ω, and 5 Ω are connected in series across a 10 V battery. What is the equivalent resistance of the combination? State the formula used.
In a series circuit with two resistors R_1 and R_2 connected to a battery, the current through R_1 is measured as 0.5 A. What is the current through R_2? Explain why.
A 12 V battery is connected to three resistors in series: R_1 = 4 Ω, R_2 = 6 Ω, R_3 = 2 Ω. Calculate (a) equivalent resistance, (b) circuit current, (c) voltage across R_2.

cards.title: In a parallel combination of resistors…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: In a parallel combination of resistors, the potential difference (voltage) across each resistor is the same, and the total current divides among the branches. The equivalent resistance (R_eq) of resistors connected in parallel is given by the reciprocal of the sum of the reciprocals of individual resistances. Its SI unit is ohm (Ω). For n resistors R₁, R₂, ..., Rₙ connected in parallel: 1/R_eq = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + ... + 1/Rₙ. The equivalent resistance is always less than the smallest individual resistance in the combination.
steps: Observe the electrical outlets in your classroom or home — the fan, lights, and computer are all connected across the same 230 V supply but operate independently
switching off the fan does not turn off the lights
This is a parallel connection: each appliance gets the full voltage
Recall from Class 6 (c6_physics_ch03_018) that parallel circuits provide multiple paths for current
Now, using Ohm's law (c10_phy_cbse_01_003) and the fact that voltage is common across parallel branches, we derive the equivalent resistance
Step 1: Write total current I = I₁ + I₂ + ..
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like R_eq = R₁ + R₂ + R₃ reveals the student is confusing parallel with series combination…
remember: State the formula for the equivalent resistance of three resistors R₁, R₂, R₃ connected in parallel. Write the SI unit of equivalent resistance.
Two resistors of 6 Ω and 3 Ω are connected in parallel across a 12 V….
Three resistors of 2 Ω, 4 Ω, and 4 Ω are connected in parallel across a 12 V….

cards.title: Joule's Law states that the heat produced in a conductor is directly…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Joule's Law states that the heat produced in a conductor is directly proportional to the square of the current passing through it, the resistance of the conductor, and the time for which the current flows, provided the physical conditions (temperature, dimensions) of the conductor remain constant. The SI unit of heat energy is joule (J).
steps: Start by asking the student to touch a mobile phone charger after it has been plugged in for 10 minutes — it feels warm
Then touch the charging cable — it is cooler
Ask: "Why does the charger get hot but the cable doesn't, even though the same current flows through both?" This observation leads to the realisation that heat depends on resistance too
Connect to Class 8 (c8_physics_ch2_6) where they saw a wire getting hot, and Class 9 (c9_physics_ch4_1) where work done by a battery equals energy transferred
Guide them to derive: Work done = VIt = (IR)It = I²Rt
Emphasise that this heat is the energy dissipated when electrons collide with lattice ions.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., writing H = IRT or H = VI²t) reveals the student has memorised the formula incorrectly and does not understand the square dependence on current.

cards.title: The heating effect of electric current is utilized in appliances where…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The heating effect of electric current is utilized in appliances where electrical energy is deliberately converted into heat energy (electric heater, electric iron, geyser) or into both heat and light energy (incandescent bulb). An electric fuse is a safety device that uses the heating effect to melt and break the circuit when current exceeds a safe limit, protecting appliances and wiring from damage.
steps: Observe the electric heater in your home during winter: when you switch it on, the coil becomes red-hot and warms the room
This is the heating effect of current in action — the same principle from the previous node (c10_phy_cbse_01_008) where H = I²Rt
Now, think of the bulb in your study lamp: the filament glows white-hot, giving light but also getting very hot
That's because the tungsten filament has high resistance and high melting point
Finally, look at the fuse box near your electricity meter — a thin wire inside melts if you run too many appliances together
To solve problems on these, first identify the given voltage (usually 220 V in India), power rating (e.g., 1000 W heater), then use P = VI to find current, and R = V/I to find resistance
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "low resistance to allow more current") reveals confusion between connecting wires (which should have low resistance) and heating elements (which need high resistance).
remember: State the two essential properties of the material used for the filament of an incandescent bulb and explain why each property is necessary.
Why is the fuse wire always connected in series with the live wire of the circuit, and why must it have a low melting point but the connecting wires must have high melting points.

cards.title: Electric power is the rate at which electrical energy is consumed or dissipated…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Electric power is the rate at which electrical energy is consumed or dissipated in a circuit. It is defined by the formula P = VI, where P is power, V is voltage (potential difference), and I is current. The SI unit of power is the watt (W), where 1 W = 1 V × 1 A. Equivalent formulas: P = I²R (using Ohm's law V = IR) and P = V²/R. For commercial units, 1 kilowatt-hour (kWh) = 3.6 × 10⁶ J, which is the unit of electrical energy consumption measured by electricity meters.
steps: When you turn on a 100 W bulb, it consumes 100 joules of energy every second
The power rating tells you the rate of energy consumption
From P = VI: if the bulb operates at 220 V (household voltage in India) and draws current I, then P = 220 × I = 100 W, so I = 100/220 ≈ 0.45 A
The three formulas are interchangeable: P = VI (direct), P = I²R (when you know current and resistance), P = V²/R (when you know voltage and resistance)
For electricity bills: energy = power × time
A 100 W bulb running for 10 hours uses E = 100 × 10 = 1000 Wh = 1 kWh = 1 unit of electricity
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "power is energy") confuses power (rate) with energy (total).
remember: Define electric power and state its SI unit.
State the three equivalent formulas for electric power.
A bulb rated 60 W operates at 220 V. Find the current drawn and the resistance of the bulb.

cards.title: Word problems combining Ohm's Law, electric power…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Word problems combining Ohm's Law, electric power, and heating effect require the simultaneous application of V = IR, P = VI = I²R = V²/R, and H = I²Rt = VIt = Pt to solve for unknown electrical quantities in real-world circuits, where the heat energy produced (in joules) or power rating (in watts) of appliances is linked to the current, voltage, resistance, and time of operation.
steps: Imagine you switch on a 2000 W electric geyser connected to a 230 V household supply in an Indian bathroom — you notice the water heats up in minutes, but have you wondered how much current it draws, what the resistance…
Recall that power P = VI gives current I = P/V, then Ohm's Law V = IR gives resistance R = V/I, and energy consumed = Pt (in joules) or P(kW) × t(h) in kWh (units)
Always convert time to seconds for joules or hours for kWh
The key is to move fluidly between P=VI, V=IR, and H=Pt depending on which variables are known and unknown.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., 22000 A or 0.4545 W) reveals the student either multiplied instead of divided, or confused the unit of current (ampere) with the unit of power (watt), indicating a lack of unit awareness and formula rearrangement skill.
remember: A 100 W, 220 V electric bulb is connected to a 220 V supply. What is the current drawn by the bulb? State the formula used and the SI unit of the answer.
Explain why the formula H = I²Rt (Joule's heating) and H = Pt give the same heat energy for a resistor, and under what condition this equivalence holds.

cards.title: A magnetic field is the region around a magnet or a current-carrying conductor…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: A magnetic field is the region around a magnet or a current-carrying conductor where a magnetic force can be experienced by another magnet, a magnetic material (like iron), or a moving charge. It is a vector quantity represented by magnetic field lines, where the tangent at any point gives the direction of the field and the density of lines indicates the field strength. The SI unit of magnetic field (magnetic flux density) is tesla (T), equivalent to newton per ampere-metre (N A⁻¹ m⁻¹).
steps: Begin with a real-world observation: sprinkle iron filings on a sheet of paper placed over a bar magnet — the filings align in curved patterns revealing the invisible magnetic field
Connect this to Class 8 where students saw a compass needle deflect near a current-carrying wire (c8_physics_ch2_1)
Now introduce the formal concept: the space around the magnet where the needle experiences a force is the magnetic field
Explain that we represent this field using imaginary lines called magnetic field lines
Demonstrate how to trace them using a plotting compass: place it near the magnet, mark the needle's north pole position, move the compass so its south pole touches the previous north mark, and repeat
Emphasize that the direction of the field at any point is the direction a free north pole would move — this is why field lines emerge from the north pole and enter the south pole externally
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "lines go from south to north outside" or "closeness indicates direction only") reveals confusion between the external and internal field direction, or a misunderstanding that field line density represents magnitude, not just direction.
remember: What is the direction of magnetic field lines outside a bar magnet, and what does the closeness of field lines indicate about the magnetic field strength.
Two magnetic field lines are drawn intersecting each other in a student's….
A student draws magnetic field lines for a bar magnet as straight lines radiating outward from the north pole and inward to the south….

cards.title: A current-carrying straight conductor produces a magnetic field in the…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: A current-carrying straight conductor produces a magnetic field in the surrounding space whose field lines form concentric circles centered on the wire, with direction given by Maxwell's right-hand thumb rule: if the thumb points in the direction of conventional current (positive to negative), the curled fingers show the direction of magnetic field lines. The magnitude of magnetic field B at a perpendicular distance r from an infinitely long straight conductor carrying current I is B = (μ₀I)/(2πr), where μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T·m/A is the permeability of free space.
steps: Begin with a real observation: place a compass near a straight wire connected to a battery — the needle deflects and aligns tangentially to circles around the wire
This mirrors the Class 8 activity (c8_physics_ch2_2) but now we quantify it

Connect to c10_phy_cbse_02_001: just as magnetic field lines around a bar magnet have direction and density indicating strength, here the concentric circles' spacing shows field strength decreases with distance
Introduce the right-hand thumb rule using the student's own right hand — thumb along current, fingers curl in field direction
Derive the inverse-distance dependence by comparing compass deflection at different distances
Finally, introduce B = μ₀I/(2πr) as the quantitative expression, emphasizing μ₀ is a universal constant like ε₀ in electrostatics.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., north) reveals the student either reverses the right-hand rule (uses left hand) or misapplies the rule by thinking field lines point radially outward like electric field from a positive charge.

cards.title: The magnetic field at the centre of a current-carrying circular loop is a…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The magnetic field at the centre of a current-carrying circular loop is a vector quantity directed perpendicular to the plane of the loop, with magnitude given by \( B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2R} \) for a single turn, where \( \mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \, \text{T·m/A} \) is the permeability of free space, \( I \) is the current in amperes, and \( R \) is the radius of the loop in metres. For a coil of \( N \) turns, the magnitude becomes \( B = \frac{\mu_0 N I}{2R} \). The direction is determined by the right-hand thumb rule: if the fingers of the right hand curl in the direction of current, the extended thumb points in the direction of the magnetic field inside the loop.
steps: Begin with a real-world observation: take a circular copper wire loop (like a bangle) connected to a battery through a switch, and place a compass needle at its centre
When the switch is closed, the compass needle deflects perpendicular to the plane of the loop — this shows a magnetic field is produced
Connect this to the prior node (c10_phy_cbse_02_002) where a straight wire produced concentric circular field lines
here the wire is bent into a loop, so the field lines become nearly straight and uniform at the centre
Demonstrate the right-hand thumb rule: curl the fingers of the right hand along the current direction
the thumb points to the magnetic field direction inside the loop
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., forgetting to convert cm to m, or using \( \mu_0/4\pi \) instead of \( \mu_0 \)) reveals the student either mishandles unit conversion or confuses the formula with that of a straight wire (\( \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r} \)).
remember: A circular loop of radius 5 cm carries a current of 2 A. What is the magnitude of the magnetic field at its centre? (Take \( \mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \, \text{T·m/A} \)).

cards.title: A solenoid is a long helical coil of insulated copper wire that produces a…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: A solenoid is a long helical coil of insulated copper wire that produces a nearly uniform magnetic field inside it when electric current passes through it, with field lines parallel to its axis and resembling those of a bar magnet. An electromagnet is a temporary magnet formed by placing a soft iron core inside a current-carrying solenoid, which magnetizes the core strongly only while current flows.
steps: Observe a doorbell or an electric crane lifting scrap metal — both use electromagnets
Start by recalling the magnetic field around a circular loop (c10_phy_cbse_02_003): each turn produces concentric circles
Now imagine stacking many such loops side-by-side to form a solenoid
the field lines inside merge into straight parallel lines
Use the right-hand grip rule: curl fingers in current direction, thumb points to the north pole
Insert a soft iron nail into the solenoid — it becomes a strong magnet only while current flows
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "field lines are circular inside") reveals confusion between a single loop and a solenoid; the student has not visualized the superposition of fields from multiple turns.
remember: State the direction of the magnetic field inside a long solenoid carrying current, and name the rule used to determine the polarity of its ends.

cards.title: The force experienced by a current-carrying conductor placed in a uniform…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The force experienced by a current-carrying conductor placed in a uniform magnetic field is given by \( F = B I L \sin\theta \), where \( B \) is the magnetic field strength (tesla, T), \( I \) is the current (ampere, A), \( L \) is the length of the conductor inside the field (metre, m), and \( \theta \) is the angle between the direction of current and the magnetic field. The direction of the force is perpendicular to both the current and the magnetic field, determined by Fleming's left-hand rule.
steps: Observe a ceiling fan in your classroom: when switched on, the motor rotates because current-carrying coils experience a force in the magnetic field of the permanent magnets
Begin by recalling that a current-carrying wire produces its own magnetic field (c10_phy_cbse_02_002)
When this wire is placed in an external magnetic field, the two fields interact, exerting a force on the wire
To quantify this, we perform a simple experiment: suspend a copper rod between the poles of a horseshoe magnet, pass current through it, and observe the displacement
The displacement is maximum when the rod is perpendicular to the field and zero when parallel
This leads to the formula \( F = BIL\sin\theta \)
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., missing \( \sin\theta \), confusing units, or writing \( F = BIL \) without the angle) reveals the student does not understand the vector nature of the force or the condition for maximum/minimum force.
remember: State the formula for the force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field. Define each symbol and its SI unit.

cards.title: A domestic electric circuit is a parallel arrangement of electrical appliances…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: A domestic electric circuit is a parallel arrangement of electrical appliances connected to a 220 V AC mains supply through three wires: the live wire (brown/red) which carries alternating current at high potential (220 V) from the supply, the neutral wire (blue/black) which completes the circuit by providing a return path at near‑zero potential, and the earth wire (green/yellow) which connects the metallic body of appliances to the ground to safely divert any leakage current and prevent electric shock.
steps: Observe the three‑pin plug of a refrigerator or iron in your kitchen — you will see three wires of different colours entering the plug

Start by asking: "Why are there three wires when a simple circuit needs only two?" Connect this to the Class 6 idea of a complete circuit (live and neutral) and the Class 8 concept of the electric fuse as a safety device
Then introduce the third wire — earth — as an additional safety path that carries fault current away from the user
Finally, summarise the rule: "Switch and fuse always go in the live wire
appliances connect across live and neutral
earth connects to the metal body."
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., swapping live/neutral colours or stating neutral is at 220 V) reveals confusion between the current‑carrying conductors and the safety conductor, and indicates the student cannot identify which wire is dangerous to touch.

Explain why the fuse and the main switch are always connected in the live wire and never in the neutral wire in household wiring.

cards.title: An electric fuse is a safety device consisting of a short length of wire made…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: An electric fuse is a safety device consisting of a short length of wire made of a low-melting-point alloy (like tin-lead or copper) that melts and breaks the circuit when the current exceeds a specified safe value due to short circuit or overloading, thereby protecting appliances and preventing fire hazards. Short circuit protection refers to the mechanism where the fuse (or MCB) interrupts the dangerously high current that flows when live and neutral wires come into direct contact, bypassing the load resistance.
steps: Observe the fuse box in your home — you will see small ceramic holders with thin wires or cartridge fuses labeled 5A, 10A, 15A
Start by recalling Class 8 learning: when current passes through a wire, heat is produced (H = I²Rt)
The fuse wire is chosen so that at normal current it stays solid, but if current suddenly rises (short circuit) or stays high too long (overloading), the heat melts it
Connect this to the domestic circuit node (c10_phy_cbse_02_006): the fuse is always placed in the live wire before the appliance

End with the key selection rule: Fuse rating (in Amperes) must be slightly higher than the normal working current of the appliance (I = P/V) but lower than the maximum safe current the wiring can carry.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., giving unit as watt or calorie) reveals the student confuses heat energy with power or uses non-SI units, which loses marks in board exams where SI units are mandatory.
remember: State the SI unit of the physical quantity that determines the heat produced in a fuse wire according to Joule's law of….
A fuse wire is rated 5 A.….

cards.title: Electromagnetic induction is the phenomenon where a changing magnetic flux…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Electromagnetic induction is the phenomenon where a changing magnetic flux through a closed conducting loop induces an electromotive force (emf) in the loop; the magnitude of the induced emf equals the rate of change of magnetic flux linkage (Faraday's Second Law), and its direction opposes the change in flux (Lenz's Law). The SI unit of induced emf is volt (V), magnetic flux is weber (Wb), and magnetic flux density is tesla (T).
steps: Observe a bicycle dynamo lighting a bulb as you pedal — the faster you pedal, the brighter the bulb
This shows mechanical energy converting to electrical energy without any battery
Begin by recalling that a current-carrying wire produces a magnetic field (c10_phy_cbse_02_002)
now we reverse the process: a changing magnetic field produces current
Measure the deflection in a galvanometer when a bar magnet is moved towards/away from a coil — the deflection exists only while the magnet moves, proving that change in magnetic flux is essential
Connect this to magnetic flux Φ = BA cosθ (from c10_phy_cbse_02_001) and state Faraday's Law: induced emf = -N (ΔΦ/Δt)
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., stating unit as tesla or writing emf = ΔΦ/Δt without N) reveals the student confuses magnetic flux density (B) with flux (Φ) or forgets the number of turns factor.
remember: State Faraday's Second Law of Electromagnetic Induction and write the formula for the magnitude of induced emf in a coil of N turns. What is the SI unit of magnetic flux.

cards.title: An electric motor is a device that converts electrical energy into mechanical…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: An electric motor is a device that converts electrical energy into mechanical energy of rotation. It operates on the principle that a current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field experiences a mechanical force whose direction is given by Fleming's left-hand rule. When a rectangular coil carrying current is placed in a uniform magnetic field, the forces on its opposite arms form a couple that produces a torque, causing continuous rotation if the current direction is reversed every half-turn by a commutator.
steps: Observe a ceiling fan or a mixer grinder in your kitchen — when you switch it on, electrical energy makes the blades rotate
This rotation is produced by an electric motor inside
To understand how, recall from c10_phy_cbse_02_005 that a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field experiences a force
Now imagine a rectangular loop of wire placed between the poles of a magnet
When current flows through the loop, the two long arms (perpendicular to the field) experience equal and opposite forces, creating a turning effect
But after half a rotation, the forces would reverse and try to stop the coil — unless we reverse the current direction at that exact moment
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "mechanical to electrical" or "Fleming's right-hand rule") reveals confusion between a motor and a generator, or between the motor rule and the generator rule — a very common board exam trap.
remember: State the energy conversion that takes place in an electric motor. Name the rule used to find the direction of force on the coil arms.

cards.title: An electric generator is a device that converts mechanical energy into…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: An electric generator is a device that converts mechanical energy into electrical energy by rotating a coil in a uniform magnetic field, inducing an alternating emf (AC generator) or a unidirectional emf (DC generator) based on electromagnetic induction. The induced emf magnitude is given by Faraday's law: ε = -dΦ/dt, where Φ = NBA cos θ is the magnetic flux through the coil.
steps: Observe a hand-cranked flashlight or a bicycle dynamo — when you rotate the handle/pedal, the bulb lights up without any battery
This is mechanical energy (rotation) becoming electrical energy
Start by recalling Faraday's law from node c10_phy_cbse_02_008: a changing magnetic flux induces emf
In a generator, we achieve this change by mechanically rotating a coil in a magnetic field
Use Fleming's right-hand rule (thumb = motion, forefinger = field, middle finger = induced current) to find current direction at each instant
For AC generator, slip rings maintain continuous contact giving alternating output
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., citing Fleming's left-hand rule or motor principle) reveals confusion between motor and generator — the left-hand rule is for force on a current-carrying conductor (motor), while the right-hand rule is for induced current due to motion…
remember: State the fundamental principle on which an electric generator works and name the rule used to determine the direction of induced current in the rotating coil.

cards.title: Fossil fuels are non-renewable energy sources formed from the decomposed…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Fossil fuels are non-renewable energy sources formed from the decomposed remains of ancient plants and animals buried under sediment over millions of years, primarily coal and petroleum, which store chemical energy that is released as heat upon combustion. Their energy content is quantified by calorific value (heat energy produced per unit mass, J/kg), and they are the dominant conventional sources for electricity generation, transportation, and industrial heating.
steps: Begin with a real-world observation: when you see a coal-fired stove in a roadside tea stall or a petrol pump on a highway, you are witnessing the end-use of energy stored millions of years ago
Ask students to trace the energy path: sunlight → photosynthesis in ancient plants → chemical energy in biomass → geological compression → coal/petroleum → combustion → heat → useful work
Connect this to Class 9's law of conservation of energy (c9_physics_ch4_8) and forms of energy (c9_physics_ch4_4)
Then introduce calorific value as the measurable link between fuel mass and heat output, leading to the formula Calorific Value = Heat Energy / Mass of fuel.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., giving unit as J/g or confusing it with specific heat capacity) reveals the student has not internalised the per-unit-mass basis or is mixing up thermal concepts from Class 9.
remember: State the definition of calorific value of a fuel and write its SI unit.

cards.title: A thermal power plant converts the chemical energy of fossil fuels (coal, oil…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: A thermal power plant converts the chemical energy of fossil fuels (coal, oil, natural gas) into electrical energy through a sequence of energy transformations: chemical energy → heat energy → mechanical energy (steam turbine) → electrical energy (generator). A hydro power plant converts the gravitational potential energy of stored water into electrical energy: potential energy → kinetic energy (flowing water) → mechanical energy (water turbine) → electrical energy (generator). Both plants operate on the principle of electromagnetic induction where a turbine rotates a generator to produce alternating current.
steps: Observe the electricity powering your home — it travels through transmission lines from a power plant
In India, when you switch on a fan, there is a 70% chance that electricity came from a thermal plant burning coal, and a 12% chance from a hydro plant
Begin by recalling Class 9 work-energy theorem (c9_physics_ch4_3) and the principle of electromagnetic induction (c8_physics_ch2_1)
Trace the energy path: for thermal, coal burns in a boiler → water becomes high-pressure steam → steam spins turbine → turbine rotates generator coil in magnetic field → AC current produced
For hydro, water stored at height in dam → flows through penstock → strikes turbine blades → generator produces electricity
The key formula linking them is efficiency = (Electrical energy output / Input energy from fuel or water) × 100%.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., skipping the boiler or turbine, or saying chemical directly to electrical) reveals the student does not understand the intermediate energy forms and the role of each…
remember: State the sequence of energy conversions in a coal-based thermal power plant, starting from the chemical energy of coal and ending with electrical….

cards.title: Improvements in technology for using conventional energy refer to advancements…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Improvements in technology for using conventional energy refer to advancements in combustion processes, pollution control systems, and energy conversion efficiency that increase the useful energy output per unit of fossil fuel consumed while reducing harmful emissions. These technologies include supercritical/ultra-supercritical steam parameters in thermal power plants, fluidized bed combustion, electrostatic precipitators, flue gas desulfurization, and improved cookstoves, all operating within the constraints of the law of conservation of energy.
steps: Observe a traditional chulha (mud stove) in a village kitchen producing thick smoke versus a modern LPG stove with a blue flame — the LPG stove represents improved technology for using conventional fuel (LPG is derived…
Start by recalling Class 9 efficiency definition: η = (Useful Output Energy / Input Energy) × 100%
Measure the concept by comparing a 1970s thermal power plant (33% efficiency) with a modern ultra-supercritical plant (45% efficiency)

Connect to prior node c10_phy_cbse_03_002 where thermal plant working was studied — now we ask: "How do we get more electricity from the same coal?" The key principle is reducing irreversibilities in the Rankine cycle…
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., 65% or 0.35 without %) reveals the student either confuses efficiency with losses (100% - η) or forgets to multiply by 100 for percentage representation — a common board exam marking penalty.

cards.title: Solar energy is the radiant energy emitted by the Sun in the form of…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Solar energy is the radiant energy emitted by the Sun in the form of electromagnetic waves (heat and light) that can be harnessed using devices like solar cookers, solar water heaters, and solar cells to perform useful work such as heating, cooking, or generating electricity. A solar device is any technology that captures and converts solar radiation into thermal or electrical energy for practical applications.
steps: Begin with a real-world observation: notice how a car parked in the summer sun becomes extremely hot inside, or how water in a black pipe on a rooftop gets warm
Ask students why the car interior heats up — this leads to the greenhouse effect
Connect this to Class 6 learning about radiation (heat without a medium) and black surfaces absorbing heat better
Then introduce the solar cooker as a device that traps this heat using a glass cover (greenhouse effect) and black interior
Next, show a solar water heater on a typical Indian rooftop and explain how it uses the same principle to heat water for bathing
Finally, introduce solar cells as devices that directly convert light energy into electrical energy, linking to Class 6 electric cells and Class 9 forms of energy
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "solar energy comes from burning fuel" or naming "solar fan" as a standard device) reveals the student confuses solar energy with other energy sources or cannot recall standard textbook devices.

cards.title: Energy from the sea refers to the harnessing of three distinct forms of…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Energy from the sea refers to the harnessing of three distinct forms of renewable energy stored in oceans: Tidal Energy (gravitational potential energy of water raised by lunar/solar gravitational pull), Wave Energy (kinetic and potential energy of surface waves generated by wind), and Ocean Thermal Energy Conversion (OTEC) (thermal energy from the temperature gradient between warm surface water and cold deep water). All three are renewable, predictable (tidal) or continuous (OTEC), and produce no direct greenhouse gas emissions during operation.
steps: Imagine standing on the shore at Mandvi Beach, Gujarat: you see the sea level rise and fall twice a day (tides), waves crashing continuously (wave energy), and feel the warm surface water while divers report icy cold…
Start with tides: Recall Class 9 gravitational potential energy (mgh) — the Moon’s gravity lifts a massive volume of water
a barrage traps this water at high tide, creating a hydraulic head
Then waves: Wind transfers kinetic energy to water particles
an oscillating water column (OWC) uses this motion to compress air and drive a turbine
Finally OTEC: Connect to Class 7 convection (land/sea breeze) — a temperature difference of just 20°C can vaporise a low-boiling-point fluid (ammonia) to run a turbine
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "tides are caused by wind" or "1 metre range is enough") reveals confusion between tidal and wave energy, or ignorance of the high capital cost needing large hydraulic head.

cards.title: Geothermal energy is the thermal energy generated and stored within the Earth's…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Geothermal energy is the thermal energy generated and stored within the Earth's crust due to radioactive decay of minerals and residual heat from planetary formation, which can be harnessed by drilling wells to access steam or hot water for direct heating or electricity generation via turbines.
steps: Observe hot springs at Manikaran (Himachal Pradesh) or Tattapani (Chhattisgarh) where groundwater heated by deep Earth emerges naturally — this visible phenomenon is the surface expression of geothermal energy

Begin by recalling Class 7 heat transfer (convection in fluids) and Class 9 work-energy theorem: heat from Earth's interior (source) → fluid convection (transfer) → turbine kinetic energy (conversion) → electrical…
Identify the three essential geological ingredients: heat source (magma/radioactive rocks), reservoir (permeable rock holding fluid), and cap rock (impermeable seal)
Connect to sibling node c10_phy_cbse_03_005 (ocean thermal) — both exploit temperature differences, but geothermal uses Earth's internal heat rather than solar-heated surface water
End with the key principle: sustainable extraction requires heat recharge rate ≥ extraction rate.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., citing only volcanic activity or solar heating) reveals confusion between geothermal (Earth-internal) and other renewable sources; omitting radioactive decay shows ignorance of the dominant continuous heat production mechanism.
remember: State the two primary sources of Earth's internal heat that make geothermal energy possible, and give the typical geothermal gradient value (°C/km) in tectonically stable regions.

cards.title: Nuclear fission is the process in which a heavy nucleus (such as uranium-235)…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Nuclear fission is the process in which a heavy nucleus (such as uranium-235) splits into two or more lighter nuclei when bombarded with a slow neutron, releasing a tremendous amount of energy due to the conversion of mass defect into energy as per Einstein's mass-energy equivalence (E = Δmc²). Nuclear fusion is the process in which two light nuclei (such as isotopes of hydrogen) combine at extremely high temperatures and pressures to form a heavier nucleus, also releasing energy because the mass of the product nucleus is less than the sum of the masses of the reactant nuclei.
steps: Begin with a real-world observation: the Sun shining in the sky and a nuclear power plant like Tarapur or Kudankulam generating electricity
Both release energy from atomic nuclei, but through opposite processes
Connect to the Class 9 concept of conservation of energy (c9_physics_ch4_8) — energy cannot be created, so where does this colossal energy come…
In nuclear reactions, the total mass of products is slightly less than the total mass of reactants
this "missing mass" (mass defect) is converted into energy
Show a slow-motion animation of a neutron striking U-235 causing fission, releasing 2-3 neutrons and ~200 MeV
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., wrong isotopes, missing neutrons, or incorrect atomic numbers) reveals the student does not conserve both mass number and atomic number in nuclear equations — a fundamental requirement for board exam nuclear reaction questions.
remember: State the exact nuclear equation for the fission of uranium-235 when bombarded with a thermal neutron, producing barium-141 and krypton-92. Include the number of neutrons released.
Explain why nuclear fusion reactions require temperatures of the order of 10⁷ K, whereas nuclear fission can be initiated at room temperature with thermal neutrons.
In a fission reaction, the mass defect is measured as 0.215 u. Calculate the energy released in joules. (Given: 1 u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s).

cards.title: Environmental consequences of energy sources refer to the detrimental effects…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Environmental consequences of energy sources refer to the detrimental effects on air, water, soil, and ecosystems resulting from the extraction, conversion, and utilization of energy resources, including greenhouse gas emissions, particulate pollution, radioactive waste, habitat destruction, and thermal pollution.
steps: Observe the thick smog over Delhi in winter or the ash pond near a local thermal power plant — these are visible consequences of burning coal
Begin by listing all energy sources studied (coal, petroleum, natural gas, nuclear, solar, wind, hydro, biomass)
For each, identify the primary pollutant or environmental stressor: CO₂ and particulates for fossil fuels
radioactive waste for nuclear
land use and habitat loss for hydro
manufacturing toxicity for solar panels
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., naming CO₂ or CO) reveals the student confuses greenhouse gases with acid rain precursors — a specific board exam trap where SO₂/NOₓ are the required keywords for acid rain questions.
remember: Name the two major gaseous pollutants released during combustion of coal in a thermal power plant that contribute to acid rain.
Explain why nuclear energy is considered a low-carbon source but still poses a long-term environmental hazard that fossil fuels do not.

cards.title: Renewable energy sources are those that are naturally replenished on a human…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Renewable energy sources are those that are naturally replenished on a human timescale (e.g., solar, wind, hydro, biomass) and have negligible depletion risk, whereas non-renewable energy sources (e.g., coal, petroleum, natural gas, nuclear fission fuels) exist in finite geological reserves and deplete irreversibly with extraction. The choice between them involves evaluating energy density, environmental impact (CO₂ emissions, habitat disruption), economic viability (capital vs. operational cost), and reliability (intermittency vs. base-load capability).
steps: Begin with a real-world observation: a rooftop solar panel on a neighbor's house and a diesel generator running during a power cut in the same locality

Ask: "Both provide electricity, but why does the solar panel have no fuel tank while the generator needs constant diesel refills?" Connect to Class 9 Work-Energy chapter (c9_physics_ch4_8: Law of Conservation of Energy)…
the source determines if the 'fuel' runs out
Guide students to list all energy sources studied so far (coal, petroleum, solar, wind, hydro, nuclear, tidal, geothermal, biomass)
Group them by asking: "Which of these will run out if we use them continuously for 100 years?" This leads to the renewability definition
Then introduce a 5-criteria comparison matrix (Availability, Energy Density, Environmental Impact, Cost, Reliability) and practice filling it for Solar vs
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "Renewable means it doesn't cause pollution") reveals the student confuses renewability with cleanliness — a common error where nuclear fission (low CO₂ but finite uranium) or biomass (renewable but emits CO₂ when burnt) are…
remember: State the defining criterion that classifies an energy source as 'renewable' according to CBSE Class 10 NCERT. Give one example each of renewable and non-renewable source.

cards.title: Energy conservation refers to the practice of reducing energy consumption by…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Energy conservation refers to the practice of reducing energy consumption by using energy more efficiently or by reducing the use of energy services, while maintaining the same level of output or comfort; it is measured in joules (J) or kilowatt-hours (kWh) saved over a period of time.
steps: Start by observing a typical Indian household: a ceiling fan running in an empty room, an incandescent bulb glowing during daytime, and a geyser left on for hours
Ask the student to identify the energy source (electricity) and trace it back to coal-fired thermal power plants studied in c10_phy_cbse_03_002
Connect this to the Class 9 concept of law of conservation of energy (c9_physics_ch4_8) — energy cannot be created, only converted, and every conversion wastes some energy as heat
Then introduce the idea that reducing wastage at the point of use means less coal burnt, less CO₂ emitted, and lower electricity bills
Finally, guide the student to list methods they can adopt today, and show how to calculate savings using power ratings and usage time.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "to save money only" or "unit is watt") reveals the student confuses energy with power or overlooks the environmental and resource-depletion aspects.
remember: State the primary reason why energy conservation is needed in India, and give the SI unit for measuring electrical energy consumption in households.
Explain why replacing a 60 W incandescent bulb with a 9 W LED bulb that gives the same brightness conserves energy, even though both are connected to the same 230 V supply.

cards.title: The laws of reflection state that…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: The laws of reflection state that: (1) The angle of incidence (∠i) is equal to the angle of reflection (∠r), and (2) The incident ray, the reflected ray, and the normal to the reflecting surface at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane. These laws are universally valid for all reflecting surfaces — plane, concave, or convex — and form the foundation for ray optics in Class 10.
steps: Begin with a real-world observation: ask students to look at their reflection in a steel spoon (concave side) and the back of the spoon (convex side) — they see distorted images, yet the basic "bouncing" behaviour of…
Connect this to Class 7/8 where they verified laws of reflection using a plane mirror and pins
Now, extend the concept: at any point on a curved mirror, draw the tangent plane
the normal is perpendicular to this tangent
The laws of reflection apply exactly at that point
This local-plane approximation is the key bridge to spherical mirrors
cards.misconception: A wrong answer reveals if the student omits the normal in the second law (common error: listing only incident and reflected rays) or confuses the plane of incidence with the plane of the mirror surface.
remember: State the two laws of reflection. For the second law, name the three elements that must lie in the same plane.

cards.title: A spherical mirror is a reflecting surface that forms part of a hollow sphere…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: A spherical mirror is a reflecting surface that forms part of a hollow sphere of glass, where reflection occurs either from the inner concave surface (concave mirror) or the outer convex surface (convex mirror). The key terms are: Pole (P) – the geometric centre of the reflecting surface; Centre of Curvature (C) – the centre of the sphere of which the mirror is a part; Radius of Curvature (R) – the distance PC; Principal Axis – the line joining P and C; Principal Focus (F) – the point on the principal axis where incident rays parallel to the axis converge (concave) or appear to diverge from (convex) after reflection; Focal Length (f) – the distance PF, where f = R/2 for both types under the paraxial approximation.
steps: Observe the rear-view mirror on a motorcycle or car — it shows a wider field of view but makes objects appear smaller and farther
that is a convex mirror
Now look at a shiny steel spoon: the inner curved side acts like a concave mirror and can form a magnified image of your face when held close

Start by identifying the reflecting surface — is it the inner (concave) or outer (convex) side of the spherical shell? Connect to Class 8 learning (c8_physics_ch6_1, c8_physics_ch6_2) where you named the parts
now apply the Cartesian sign convention: all distances measured from the pole, positive along incident light direction, negative opposite
Derive f = R/2 geometrically using a paraxial ray and the law of reflection (c10_phy_cbse_04_001), noting that the approximation sin θ ≈ θ requires small aperture
cards.misconception: A wrong answer revealing confusion between "real focus" and "virtual focus" or sign convention reversal indicates the student has not internalised the Cartesian sign convention (distances measured from pole, positive along incident light).
remember: Define the principal focus of a concave mirror and a convex mirror. State the sign of the focal length for each according to the Cartesian sign convention.

cards.title: Image formation by a concave mirror is the process of locating the position…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Image formation by a concave mirror is the process of locating the position, size, nature (real or virtual), and orientation (erect or inverted) of the image formed when light rays from an object reflect off the concave mirror's surface, constructed using any two of the three principal rays: (1) ray parallel to principal axis reflects through focus, (2) ray passing through centre of curvature reflects back along same path, (3) ray passing through focus reflects parallel to principal axis.
steps: Observe the concave mirror in your school laboratory or a shiny metal spoon's inner surface — notice how your reflection appears inverted when the spoon is held at arm's length but becomes erect and magnified when…
This real-world observation reveals that image characteristics change dramatically with object distance
Begin by recalling the three principal rays from Class 8 (c8_physics_ch6_5) and the mirror terminology from the previous node (c10_phy_cbse_04_002)
Draw the principal axis, mark P, F, C at correct scale (f = R/2)
For each object position, draw any two principal rays, locate their intersection (or apparent intersection for virtual images), and measure image distance and size relative to object
Always verify: real images form where reflected rays actually meet (in front of mirror), virtual images form where reflected rays appear to diverge from (behind mirror).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., choosing ray through F as one of the two) reveals the student doesn't recognize that a ray through F reflects parallel to axis, making intersection harder to locate at C, or they confuse the ray through C with ray through F.

cards.title: Image formation by a convex mirror occurs when incident rays parallel to the…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: Image formation by a convex mirror occurs when incident rays parallel to the principal axis appear to diverge from the principal focus (F) after reflection, and rays directed towards the centre of curvature (C) reflect back along the same path; the virtual, erect, and diminished image is formed between the pole (P) and the focus (F) for all object positions in front of the mirror.
steps: Observe the side-view mirror of a parked auto-rickshaw or car in your neighbourhood — notice how it shows a wide field of view but makes vehicles look smaller and farther away than they actually are
This is a convex mirror in action

Begin by recalling the two standard rays from Class 8 (c8_physics_ch6_6): a ray parallel to the principal axis reflects as if coming from the focus (F), and a ray heading towards the centre of curvature (C) reflects…
On a fresh sheet, draw the principal axis, mark the pole (P), focus (F), and centre of curvature (C) on the correct side (behind the mirror for convex)
Place the object upright on the principal axis in front of the mirror
Draw the two rays from the top of the object, extend the reflected rays backwards behind the mirror with dotted lines, and locate the virtual image where they appear to meet
